subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-STATEMENTS ON OUTBREAK OF HOSTILITIES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-STATEMENTS ON OUTBREAK OF HOSTILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement to the house on the situation in the Middle East. With events in that area, tragic events, unfolding rapidly and at present uncertainly, the house will not expect me to go into details even if I were able to do so.
The house is aware, I am sure, that the Secretary General of the United Nations reported this morning to the security council, which was meeting in emergency session, the outbreak of large scale hostilities on the land and in the air between the armed forces of Israel and Israel's neighbours. I understand, Mr. Speaker, that these engagements may have extended to Sharm el Sheikh on the gulf of Aqaba.
The circumstances in which fighting began are not clear, and already there have been charges and countercharges. The Secretary General this morning was not in a position to throw any light on this question on the basis of reports he had received from the United Nations truce supervisory organization chief of staff or the commander of the United Nations emergency force.
The UNTSO chief of staff, whose headquarters are in the area between the lines in Jerusalem, tried to arrange a cease fire on the Israel-Jordan border and possibly elsewhere, without success. UNTSO headquarters in Jerusalem are no longer in touch with New York. It is understood that these headquarters were occupied by Jordanian forces but, reportedly, reoccupied by Israeli forces. UNTSO headquarters may not, therefore, be able to contribute much further information at this time at least regarding the course of the fighting.
Twenty Canadian officers are serving with UNTSO; our contingent with UNEF has, of course, left the area. Members of the house will have heard, I am sure, with deep regret the Secretary General's report of the tragic
death of three members of the Indian contingent of UNEF and the wounding of others in a strafing attack in the Gaza area. There has also been a report in the last hour or so that a member of the Brazilian contingent in UNEF has been killed. These are the only casualties among the United Nations personnel of which we have any word. a (2:40 p.m.)
As hon. members know, the security council this morning heard statements by the Secretary General, the representative of Israel and the representative of the U.A.R. Urgent consultations are proceeding among the members of the council, during a recess which was called, on the text of a resolution to be introduced and, I hope, agreed on without delay, with a view to meeting the most urgent immediate requirement, which is a cease fire.
When the Secretary General made his report to the security council on his return from
Cairo a few days ago, he included these words, and I quote from his report.
My main concern at this critical juncture must be to try to gain time in order to lay the basis for a detente.
Well, some time was gained, but the security council was unable to act effectively to prevent the crisis deteriorating into war. Therefore, to repeat the Secretary General's phrase; "our main concern at this critical juncture must be to end the fighting" and, after that, to bring about an armistice which will be binding on both sides and which will stick until it can be converted into peace and a political settlement. Surely there can be no further delay or debate about this. If things once again remain unchanged after the fighting ends, the fighting will begin again at some future date. I along with others said this in 1956 and 1957, and I say it with more conviction and even with some desperation now.
But that is for the future, though I hope for the near future. For the moment the security council should concentrate, as no doubt it is doing, on ending the fighting as the only certain way of preventing it from spreading. I am not suggesting it will spread-I am not an alarmist here-but we should do everything to remove this dire and dreadful possibility. Therefore a cease fire comes first.

June 5, 1967
Middle East Crisis
This is not the time to establish responsibility, let alone to assess blame for what happened in the early hours of this morning. That kind of inquiry can wait. In any event it would have to relate the occasion of war to the cause of war, something which goes back many years and deep into basic policy.
The main responsibility for intervening to end the war and bring about a settlement rests with the security council, on which Canada serves and where we shall do everything we can to bring about peace. In particular it rests upon the four permanent members of the security council, the United Kingdom, the United States, France and the U.S.S.R. They should meet and discharge that responsibility, preferably as members of the Security Council and reporting to that body-but I feel they should meet-and perhaps on a high political level. This is a time for very deep concern. It is no time for despair, but for a great effort for peace in that area.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-STATEMENTS ON OUTBREAK OF HOSTILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Prime Minister for his statement. I agree that at this particular moment in the grave world situation one cannot go further than he has gone in saying that every possible effort should be made to bring a cessation to the fighting. Every possible effort should be made in the security council to arrange for an armistice. Only at that stage can we hope for a general settlement of the troubles that have beset the Middle East for so long.
At the present moment, with only brief details available of the extent of the fighting, it is impossible, as the Prime Minister has indicated, to assess blame or responsibility. We will have to wait and see what happens, not that waiting and seeing are always the best course when trouble breaks out in the world, but at this particular stage Canada can only hopefully express its aspirations that the security council will be able to take action and that the four major powers there, whose concern with the Middle East has been great for so many years, will make sure that the conflict is contained and stopped in the shortest possible time.
We are living in an age when we cannot face the horrors of widespread war without a great deal of fear. This is one of the grave moments in world history when we are given, we hope, another chance to reassess some of the problems of the world and, if this conflict

can be checked, try to cure some of the underlying causes of that conflict. I recall so well that in the spring of 1956 when trouble was brewing in the Middle East we had discussions here in the House of Commons. We looked to the United Nations to stop any outbreak of violence in that area, but nevertheless it did occur. In the spring of 1956 I was called upon to address a public meeting in Montreal on the state of affairs in the Middle East, and one paragraph from my address I think is applicable at the present time. I said then:
What happens to Israel at this grave juncture is a matter of great concern not only to all the small nations but to the world organization of the United Nations. For the United Nations assembly in 1947 determined the partition of Palestine, accepted the conclusion of the mandate of Great Britain and launched the tiny state on the course that led to its independence. The United States and Russia were in agreement, Canada played an active part in promoting the interests of the new nation, 33 nations voted in favour of the plan. In fact, the state of Israel is a creation of the United Nations. If the state of Israel should now be destroyed the influence and the prestige of the United Nations would suffer a serious reverse.
During the course of that address I also used these sentences:
-the establishment of the state of Israel has been marred by many acts of violence and has resulted in much bitterness and in the uprooting and dispersal of other people. Until some solution is found for the Arab refugees from Palestine the Middle East will continue to be unsettled. There is great need for an understanding of all these problems by other nations of the world.
That was 11 years ago. The situation has now reached a crisis point again and a solution still evades us. I do not know how many more lessons the world will require before we are able, through the United Nations, to settle some of these troublesome problems in the world which apparently inevitably lead to armed conflict.

Mr. Speaker, first I should like to express to the right hon. Prime Minister our appreciation for his having asked spokesmen of the parties opposite him to meet with him and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. This seems to us to be an act of statesmanship of which we approve in a crisis of this sort. Of course I know this is not the first time it has been done.
Mr. Speaker, in this most serious and dangerous situation there is surely no purpose in seeking to lay blame for the actual outbreak
June 5, 1967

of fighting. In my view the Middle East war really began the moment the UN emergency force was withdrawn and forces began to mass all around the borders of Israel and on the Israeli side.
The great world tragedy, I suggest, lies in the failure of the United Nations to reach any fruitful conclusions during the past two weeks, when it was still possible to avoid the actual outbreak of fighting. Instead of dealing with the crisis constructively and with a sense of urgency for the peace of the world, the security council became bogged down in endless debate. The actual war in the Middle East is tragic beyond words. Equally tragic is the low point to which the influence of the United Nations has been brought by the failure of the security council in this crisis.
This is, I think, a sad moment for the international organization and for the world. In our view, however, this very fact must strengthen the determination of all members of the international organization to do everything humanly possible to rebuild the influence and value of the United Nations; for it still remains the only international quorum for discussion and action to avoid disaster in the future.
I repeat what I said in the house two weeks ago tomorrow. One of the basic problems in the Middle East crisis leading to the present war has been the refusal of the Arab states to recognize Israel's right to exist. I also underline my personal conviction that when the United Nations solemnly established the state of Israel in the fall of 1947 that act, which had the full support of the Soviet union and all the great powers at that time, carried with it a moral as well as a legal obligation to seek a political settlement in the Middle East. This was not done. Indeed, even in the last ten years since the United Nations emergency force was established no steps to my knowledge were taken to follow up the end of the fighting at that time with an energetic search for a political settlement, despite the warnings of our present Prime Minister and others during the debate at the United Nations in 1957.
I mention these facts briefly because of my conviction that even if a cease fire should be achieved in the present military encounter, the danger to peace will continue to be great and ever present unless we learn from the past and follow up such cease fire with the most determined effort to establish a permanent basis for peace in that area.
I should like to say to the Prime Minister that my colleagues and I fully support the
Middle East Crisis
policy he has just outlined, namely that the security council has an immediate duty to seek a cease fire and to adopt a resolution to that effect. It is obvious to us that for the resolution to have any influence at all it must avoid any attempt to try to name anyone as the aggressor, a task which in view of the fragmentary information in the hands of the security council is as impossible as it is undesirable.
It also seems clear, and I should like to underline this if I may, that the solution, if it is to be found at all, lies in the hands of the four big powers, the four permanent members of the security council whom the Prime Minister named. If no progress appears possible at the security council, then it seems to us that a four power summit meeting or other kind of meeting is essential. It is my hope, and from the Prime Minister's words he shares this view, that Canada and all other smaller powers should encourage the bigger powers to engage is such a meeting. It is also clear, and let me emphasize this as well, that the steps both at the security council and, if necessary, at the four power meeting, should be taken without any delay.
The right hon. Prime Minister has often said that in his experience a crisis frequently makes possible solutions which might not otherwise have been possible. I hope with all my heart that he is right in the present situation, and if he is right it may be very desirable indeed that a meeting of the four big powers consider not only the immediate conflagration in the Middle East but other threats to the peace of the world, such as the war in Viet Nam.
Mankind is already too long on the brink of global disaster. If there is any real and honourable desire on the part of the big powers to lay a foundation for a genuine peace, we urge that they grasp the occasion of the unhappy situation in the Middle East to cease big power manoeuvring, which has rendered the United Nations powerless, and seek a settlement of many of the threatening fronts.
However, I want to close by emphasizing that this more long range objective must not, of course, interfere with the immediate objective to achieve a cease fire in the Middle East. I emphasize also that this should be followed by a withdrawal of all forces engaged in the present conflict, by the introduction of an appropriate United Nations presence to avoid further conflict, and by energetic steps to find a permanent solution in that area.

June 5, 1967

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier this morning, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) stated:
I am greatly concerned at the news that hostilities have started in the Middle East. At this time, all efforts must be directed to a ceasefire. There Is only one certain way to prevent the fighting from spreading and that is to end it.
I think that this is sincere advice, likely to restore peace in that part of the Middle East.
Mr. Speaker, we too, deeply regret the grave situation which is worsening and leading to a world war and we no longer know where to lay the blame.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) just said a minute ago that we do not know whether the Arabs or the state of Israel attacked first. It is not too certain, it is confusing. In any case, formal accusations indicate that Israel is guilty of aggression.
At a time when a resolution is about to be introduced, if it has not already been done, before the security council for an unconditional ceasefire, to be accepted by all nations, one great power says: We will agree provided the state of Israel is recognized as the aggressor. Objections are raised against the resolution immediately.
I sincerely believe that if all the truly responsible nations who really have world peace at heart would work hand in hand, they could, through this resolution, change the belligerent intentions of the countries concerned by exerting their influence to bring back to reason those who, today, would not balk at bringing on a world-wide conflagration which might lead to the end of the world through an atomic or nuclear war.
Mr. Speaker, the conflict we are witnessing today in the Middle East did not originate yesterday or last week, but it goes back several years.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said earlier that the conflict is due to the fact that the Arabs have always refused to recognize the existence of Israel. Now, the cause of the conflict goes back prior to that: from the time when Israel was created by the United Nations. As a matter of fact, the whole territory belonged to the Arabs who claim it was stolen from them. And it is since then that the Arabs have been trying to recover that territory which is the present state of Israel.
At any rate, since 1956, or since the second world war, there have been skirmishes in the

Middle East between Israel and Arab countries. Today, we are still facing the problem we discussed in this house in 1956.
The solution proposed by the Prime Minister is still the best. If we really want to achieve peace, let us first of all have a ceasefire, let us hold our positions, and then meet like men to hold round table discussions.
That is done at the security council. Canada plays its role and I congratulate the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) for their objective attitude in trying to settle the conflict.
I do wish that Canada will always maintain its stand of calling upon nations to get together in an effort to find common grounds so as to avoid a third world war and to help Arabs understand that their right to live is respected in the world and to help Israelites realize that they themselves have a right to live in this world, which is everybody's world, as we say.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe that the stand taken by the Canadian government with regard to this resolution for a ceasefire is a excellent one. Let us continue discussing at the diplomatic level and in a human way, so that people may realize that their interest is not to kill one another and that the countries involved may realize the importance of discussions if there is to be maintained a peace that will serve all the world's nations at the same time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the present situation is not going to be solved by a multitude of words, but I should just like to say that those in this party support the statement by the Prime Minister that the most important matter at the present time is to obtain a cease fire in the Middle East. I am sure everyone recognizes the fact that what happens in the Middle East will not just affect that immediate area but will have repercussions right across the world.
It seems to me there are two unfortunate object lessons here. One is the failure of the United Nations to resolve this problem before it reached its present proportions; the other is the blow that the concept of peace keeping has received through this unfortunate situation. I believe these two matters put together constitute a very serious situation as far as the world organization is concerned. So we support the idea that there must be a cease fire immediately, and of course coupled with that
June 5, 1967

would be the withdrawal of the various forces to their original positions.
It was stated a number of years ago that as long as the refugee problem in the Middle East remained unsolved it would continue to be a potential fuse capable of setting off a major conflict. I believe that is true, and one of the reasons we face this tragic situation today is that a political settlement was not achieved in regard to the refugee problem. In a measure this would have defused the whole situation. Without any more words said this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that we support the Prime Minister's view in this connection.

1967-1122 of June 2, 1987, the export of silver coin, silver and silver alloy in wrought or unwrought forms, chemicals, salts and compounds of silver, and silver and silver alloy scrap, to all destinations including the United States was made subject to permit control effective immediately.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ISSUE OF NICKEL COINS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR ISSUE OF NICKEL COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make an announcement to the house concerning the coinage, which is related to the announcement just made by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce concerning restrictions on the export of silver.
Issue of Nickel Coins
I stated in a press release on December 23 last that it is the intention of the government to change the composition of our present silver coinage to pure nickel. As I pointed out at that time, silver is becoming too scarce to be used as coinage. I announced in December that the government planned to introduce an amendment to the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act in order to authorize the issue of coins made of pure nickel for the 10 cent, 25 cent and 50 cent pieces.
As a result of the recent action of the United States government to confine the sales of silver to domestic users in the United States it is now necessary to conserve the supplies of silver in Canada for normal uses, including coinage. We have enough silver on hand in the mint to look after our anticipated requirements for coinage and medallions for some months. We felt it only prudent, however, in the present circumstances to provide the Royal Canadian Mint with the authority to commence the production of 10 cent and 25 cent pieces made of pure nickel so as to be ready to issue such nickel coins when appropriate. Accordingly the government has used the authority in the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act that provides for a change in the coinage at a time when the metal being used becomes scarce.
An order in council has been passed and a formal proclamation is being made to authorize the issue of 10 cent and 25 cent coins made of pure nickel. Silver coins of these values will continue to be produced and issued by the mint until such time as the new nickel coins are to be put into circulation. The mint will also continue to supply the numismatic silver coin sets and medallions that it has undertaken to sell to the public and will continue to accept orders for coin sets in accordance with the earlier announcement.
I stated last December that our plans concerning the target date for the issue of nickel coins will take into account the special requirements of the automatic vending machine industry. Since the new nickel coinage will circulate side by side with the existing silver coinage for some years, it is desirable that automatic vending machines should be able to accept both silver and nickel coins of the same face value. It is our hope, therefore, that we will be able to relate the introduction of nickel coins to the installation of new coin selector devices.

June 5, 1967

speechtext:

PROMOTIONAL EXAMINATIONS FOR OFFICERS, ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
1.	Have promotional examinations for officers been discontinued in Canada's regular forces?
2.	If so, when was this action taken and for what reasons was it taken?
3.	What is the present method and what are the criteria for promotion in Canada's armed forces?

speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Associale Minisler of National Defence):
subtopic: PROMOTIONAL EXAMINATIONS FOR OFFICERS, ARMED FORCES
speechtext: In the past, army officers were required to pass both theoretical and practical examinations to qualify for captain and major ranks. R.C.A.F. short service officers, not regular officers, had to pass theoretical examinations only, before promotion to flight lieutenant. Navy officers had no promotion examinations requirement other than to obtain a watchkeeping certificate before promotion to navy lieutenant. These inconsistencies in the promotion prerequisites of the three services have created serious inequities among officers. As a result, army and air force theoretical examinations are being terminated following completion of the 1967 series. The new common policy will permit all officers to be assessed by an annual promotion board based on: (a) merit and potential for more senior rank; (b) the serving of at least minimum specified time in rank to ensure experience and knowledge have been gained for the next higher rank, and to provide time for proper assessment of suitability for promotion; (c) recommendations of senior supervising officers.

speechtext: Order, please. House again in committee of supply, estimates of the Department of Fisheries for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1968. Vote No. 1 is to be found at page 160 of the blue book of estimates, with the details thereof listed on page 161. Shall vote 1 carry?

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in presenting the estimates of the Department of Fisheries I do not wish to take up too much of the time of the committee. As hon. members know, I covered the field quite extensively last year. Furthermore, the estimates of the department were fully discussed by the standing committee. I should like to make some general and brief remarks.
o (3:40 p.m.)
The development of the fishing industry in Canada during the past few years has been unprecedented. This government, the provincial governments and the industry have coordinated their efforts in a remarkable manner since our joint development program went into effect over three years ago. Just how remarkable is shown in the increases in the size and value of landings from 1963 to 1966. In that period landings rose by 11 per cent and their value by 35 per cent. Exports went up by 27 per cent, and the total marketed value of all fish products sold both in Canada and in the 76 countries to which we export them increased by 31 per cent. Last year's exports, with a value of more than $219 million, showed an increase for the fifth consecutive year and this year's sales to the United States, our biggest customer, are expected to reach a new record.
In departmental operations the Fisheries Development Act, introduced last year, has
June 5. 1967

been of great importance. It has allowed us to introduce new measures to facilitate progress and to extend our development activities which now reach into most sectors of the primary and processing industries. One of these I should like to mention particularly provides financial assistance for the construction or modification of cold storage facilities for frozen fishery products and for bait. This assistance is provided under the new fishery products storage regulations which are designed to improve the quality of frozen fishery products. We considered they were necessary because of the increased landings being made, especially on the Atlantic coast. This year applications will be considered for assistance toward the construction of new cold storage facilities and the installation of refrigeration equipment, as well as for modification of existing premises. When grants are approved, they may be made to cover up to one third of the building and equipment but will not exceed $150,000 in any one case.
We are involved in a great many industrial development projects ourselves, as well as with the provinces, in order to improve the efficiency of our fishing vessels, catching gear and processing plants. To meet the intensive competition from other countries we must have the most modern equipment available and we must also conduct training programs so that skilled manpower will be available to allow us to meet the challenge of the era of automation.
In the end product of our fisheries, nothing is more vital than quality control and improvement and through our revised fish inspection regulations and canned fish and shellfish inspection regulations we shall be able to implement a national inspection program designed to safeguard the quality of fish products at all stages. There is now provision for compulsory registration of processing plants, including canneries, which prepare fish and shellfish for sale outside the province of origin. Since 1965 registration requirements have established standards for plant construction, equipment and sanitation, and these are now being extended to canneries and salt fish plants. There will also be minimum standards for fishing boats, refrigerated transport and cold storages, and for closer control over the use of quality designations.
I should also mention that last year the department inaugurated the retail inspection of fishery products on an experimental basis in Montreal. This brought a very favourable response from store managers and we believe
Supply-Fisheries
an expansion of this type of inspection to other cities is justified.
In order to make available to industry the highest level of professional and technical advice for dealing with quality problems of all kinds, we are sponsoring the university training of inspectors toward a degree in science.
Canada's reputation as a producer of high quality fishery products is world wide, evidenced by the fact that we have been invited to be the host nation for an international meeting of fish inspection and quality control to be held under the auspices of F.A.O. in Halifax in June, 1969.
In the development of the fisheries we have many projects under way from coast to coast to conserve and expand resources where this is possible. Two very large programs which involve ingenious and complex engineering accomplishments in British Columbia are the Big Qualicum projects to enhance the environment of the Pacific salmon, and the construction of a system of spawning channels in the Babine river system which, when completed, will allow for an increase of 100 million sockeye salmon fry.
We have a long-range program to protect and restore runs of salmon in the Atlantic region where, as in other parts of the country, diversion of water for industrial purposes threatens the existence of a natural resource.
The vote for conservation and protection covers our usual operations, the maintenance of vessels in the department's fleet and of other establishments. Moneys are requested this year to start construction of a new, 150-foot protection vessel and for the replacement of smaller vessels in the 60- to 65-foot class.
A program in which the federal government is involved, along with the government of Newfoundland, is one which hon. members have probably heard of as the resettlement program. This has a double purpose, to provide a better and fuller life for many fishing families and to take greater advantage of the fishery resource of the northwest Atlantic.
The importance of international co-operation in the management of fisheries has long been recognized by Canada, and we hope soon to be signatory to nine international conventions. We already participate in seven. We have now applied for membership in the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission, and we are one of 18 countries which are working out details of a convention to deal with the conduct of fishing vessels in the

June 5, 1967
Supply-Fisheries
north Atlantic. The purpose of this is to increase safety at sea and prevent damage to fishing gear, especially on the crowded fishing grounds where fishing vessels of many nations operate.
The work of the Fisheries Research Board of Canada is invaluable. The results of its investigations have been applied in many ways, with great advantage to the resource and the industry. They have also made it possible for this country to more than hold its own in various internal fisheries management programs. The need for even greater research efforts is shown in our plans for expansion in several areas. There is to be a $7 million laboratory for the newly established Freshwater Institute in Winnipeg, a new research board laboratory building in St. John's, increased accommodation at the board's laboratories at Dartmouth, Halifax and Nanaimo, and a new water laboratory at West Vancouver. The board's reputation throughout the world is unmatched, c (3:50 p.m.)
I have touched only briefly on some of the more important aspects of the activities of my department so that in considering the estimates you will be acquainted with the scope of our efforts and the direction we are taking in our contribution to the orderly expansion of the fishing industry.
Recently hon. members questioned me in the house about a problem connected with a logging drive on the Stellako river in British Columbia. In recent weeks and months I have had extensive correspondence with the responsible provincial minister and, as requested by the hon. member for Skeena, I have asked that I be permitted to table this correspondence which I am sure will make clear in the minds of hon. members the problems we are facing.
I have taken the position that we should make multiple use of our waters, taking into consideration the interest of the forest industry as well as that of the fishing industry. On Friday last I received notification from the provincial minister that he was prepared to accept my proposal that a limited logging drive, controlled and supervised by both the federal and provincial authorities, be allowed on the Stellako river, with measures taken to prevent any damage to the spawning grounds. I understand that log drive is almost ready to start and will be completed probably by the middle of this month.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, a decision will be taken probably within the next few

weeks on the implementation of the straight base line system. On May 7 at the annual meeting of the Fisheries Council in Montreal I stated that an announcement to this effect would be made in the house by my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who is responsible for the administration of the act. In view of the world situation and the strain placed on my colleague during the last few weeks I am sure hon. members will realize his announcement may have to be delayed for a matter of days. I am sure hon. members will understand the position.
I was also questioned in the house by hon. members from Prince Edward Island regarding subsidies on the construction of fishing vessels. I assured them that the matter would be examined again. Early in May we made a special survey. The fishermen's loan board of the province took part in the survey. As a result, of the 96 applications which we received from that province 51 have been approved, four are still doubtful and will require further study, and the balance of 41 have been rejected, a decision concurred in by the loan board, because those applications did not meet the criteria established by the federal government and the criteria established by the provincial loan board.
I am prepared to answer later any questions which hon. members may pose.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on this occasion it is my intention to take a leaf from the minister's book and not speak extensively on the estimates of his department. The estimates of the Department of Fisheries for the preceding fiscal year were thoroughly examined less than a year ago. In fact they were referred to the standing committee on fisheries where the operations and the policies of the department were given a searching scrutiny. However, a number of members from this party will be asking specific questions and making brief statements. The notable thing about this year's estimates is that they are larger than ever before. I do not say this as a criticism. They are about $5 million more than they were last year but I believe this is justified.
The importance of the Department of Fisheries has been recognized over the years by the increasing importance of the fishing industry in our own economy and in the economy of the world. In 1952 total expenditures by the Department of Fisheries were about $9 million. Five years later, in 1957, they had increased to $13 million, and five years later, in 1962, had almost doubled to $24
June 5, 1967

million. In the last five years they have almost doubled again to reach a total of $47 million. This, of course, is not a true picture because the value of the dollar has depreciated considerably over those 15 years. But even taking constant dollars, expenditures on fisheries have increased a lot and, as I have said, I think this is justified.
We are in a phase of our development when the fishing industry is becoming more and more important. This is just another indication that the world is experiencing a population explosion. As population increases the demand for food also increases, and the demand is most noticeable with respect to protein foods. They are the scarcest. They are foods which are produced from the sea, and of course from other sources. In one sense the fishing industry represents the recovery from the sea of the proteins which have been lost from the land over milleniums of time. There is little nitrogen, the basic building block of protein, fixed in the sea. Nitrogen is fixed on land by plants and to some extent by lightning, and it is used to manufacture chemical fertilizer. The recovery of these protein foods from the sea is becoming an increasingly important factor in the diet of human beings, and the demand for these proteins to meet the needs of a hungry world will increase as time goes on.
With respect to Canada as a fishing nation I would point out that until very recently 95 per cent of the fish caught throughout the world were caught in the northern hemisphere. Recently there have been great fishing developments in parts of the southern hemisphere because of efforts by the Food and Agriculture Organization and by some southern countries such as Peru on their own initiative.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
In 1948, almost 20 years ago now, Canada ranked sixth among the ten leading fishing nations of the world. By 1965 she had slipped to tenth place principally because of the much more rapid growth in the fish landings of other countries. As an exporter of fish and fisheries' products, in 1964 Canada stood seventh in volume but second in value, partly reflecting the relatively higher value of the species being shipped and partly because of the further degree of processing and packaging in the Canadian industry. This is a very brief summary of Canada's relative position, but it brings out the point that although Canada is only the tenth fishing nation in the world now in respect of volume it is the second in respect of export value. We should
Supply-Fisheries
realize this means that Canada's position as a fishing nation is different from the position of many of the nations of the world which fish extensively. Whether it is economical or not in our terms, they must fish in order to feed their own population. We have to compete, however, in world markets for the same of our fish products and therefore we must be highly productive as a fishing nation in order to compete successfully.
In order to be more efficient there must be a greater tonnage of fish produced per man hour and this means there must be a very great increased investment in the industry. This requires the use of large-scale processing plants, larger trawlers and other types of fishing vessels which represent a very large capital investment. It means an investment for the freezing, processing and transportation of this product to world markets. Investment in the fishing industry has been going up very rapidly in the last few years. The investment is going up and must go up more rapidly than the increase in employment because the only way we can compete properly in world markets is by lowering the labour content in the product.
In many cases, as the figures indicate, our traditional fishing industry is engaged in the production of what are almost luxury products and in some cases are luxury or high-cost products where the element of labour is not so important. In this regard I might mention the lobster fishery, the salmon fishery, the oyster fishery and that type of operation. There is also the traditional groundfishing industry which has had a great deal of capital poured into it in the last number of years. This industry has increased tremendously and is important especially to Canada's east coast.
The most recent development of all, of course, is the recognition of the fact that of all the species of fish harvested perhaps the most important in world terms is the herring. Herring is the greatest available producer of protein for use by man and animal. There has been a tremendous development on the east coast in this regard. On the east coast in the last year or so ten new herring processing plants have commenced production. I believe they have a combined total capacity in the order of 6,000 tons of herring a day. This is a tremendous amount of fish.
The herring are being processed into herring oil and fish meal. The fish meal is produced almost entirely as a protein supplement for animal feeds in order to bring up the protein content in these feeds. The use of this protein for human consumption is not direct.

June 5, 1967
Supply-Fisheries
The protein is used in feed for animals and the animals in turn are consumed by human beings. If the demand for protein increases even further I think we will have to develop commercially-this has already been done for some time on an experimental basis-the direct processing of fish meal and fish flour for the feeding of humans because the human diet now in many parts of the world is deficient in the most costly element-protein.
In this connection I should say that on the east coast there are other developments in other branches of the fishing industry. I do not intend to be all-inclusive when I mention these few examples. There are new developments such as the tuna fishery based in Charlotte county, New Brunswick, the whaling industry based in Nova Scotia, the mackerel industry which is more efficiently processing mackerel for human consumption at Rustico, Prince Edward Island, the new plant at Shelburne for the processing of herring for human consumption, the plant for the production of marine plant products in Miminegash, Prince Edward Island and near Charlottetown, and many other developments in the fishing industry.
These developments, of course, are not all painless. There is the further development of the use of larger ships which can go farther out to sea and catch fish more efficiently than can be done by the traditional inshore fishery. There are many communities on the east coast of Canada especially which have come into being because of the inshore fishery. In many cases the situation for the inshore fishermen in these areas is becoming more difficult all the time.
There is a human problem involved, and this is particularly true in Newfoundland and in parts of the province of Quebec. An intention has been expressed by the province of Quebec to increase the income of the fishermen in isolated places by supporting the prices of some of these products. As I see it, the province of Quebec has a complete right to do this in the interests of the people concerned. I might add that the hon. member for Gaspe is especially interested in this matter but unavoidably had to leave the chamber this afternoon. He will be unable to make the remarks he wished to make in this regard. I wish to point out to members of the committee that this is a matter which is of interest to members of parliament from the province of Quebec and that in my judgment the provincial governments are completely within their rights in trying to do something which will
(Mr. MacLean (Queens).]
put a little more money into the pockets of our inshore fishermen, especially those who have the added disadvantage of a very short season.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I want to make a few remarks now regarding some other items of concern to the fishing industry generally. First let me mention very briefly the sealing industry on the Atlantic coast. I commend the minister for his recent sound and reasoned statement in respect of this industry. Of course everyone wants the harvesting of the seal crop to be as humane as possible, and I think this is being done at the present time as nearly as well as we can reasonably expect. We should not cease to seek improvements, but I feel reasonably sure that the herds of seals are being exploited in a rational way, at least as far as Canada is concerned, and are not being exterminated. However, this is a matter which will have to be watched closely. I know the minister realizes this and that the department has the industry under very close supervision.
In this regard I should like to make a suggestion to the minister about sealing in the gulf of St. Lawrence where aircraft are involved. I know the responsibility does not come directly under this department but under the Department of Transport. When aircraft are used in the sealing industry a tremendous financial investment is riding on whether or not an aircraft can operate on a given day and a great temptation exists to fly aircraft under weather conditions which are not fit for flying with the result that there is danger to life and equipment. It is pretty hard for an operator to refrain from operating an aircraft, even when the flying weather is not fit if somebody else is going to fly anyhow. I strongly recommend to the minister that before the next sealing season someone from the Department of Transport be appointed for the period of the seal hunt with the power to control flying in the sense that he could declare when flying had to cease or when it would not be permitted because of weather conditions. This would apply equally to all operators. It would make the operation much more safe and orderly and reduce the loss of equipment.
The minister mentioned the growing necessity for rational exploitation of the resources of the sea. This again is an element related to the increased demand for fishery products. As the demand increases the interest of the nations concerned increases, and the tendency
June 5. 1967



for conflicts to arise between nations regarding their rights and privileges is bound to be greater. Five or six years ago international conventions were agreed to at Geneva. I strongly recommend that Canada ratify the conventions she has not ratified yet so we will be recognized as having an interest in rational and orderly exploitation of the living resources of the sea.
The minister also mentioned briefly the problems regarding exclusive fishing rights for Canadians within a 12-mile zone of Canada's coasts. Three years have passed since we put through legislation empowering the government to declare a 12-mile exclusive fishing zone for Canadians and, to put it mildly, I am greatly disappointed at the lack of progress which has been made. It is not my intention, however, to press the point now as I can well understand that the Department of External Affairs, which is of course involved in this matter, has bigger fish to fry at the moment. That does not relieve the government in any way of the responsibility to find an acceptable solution to these problems at the earliest possible time and to at least declare some geographical co-ordinates in some areas in order to start this desirable process on its way.
We are, of course, a leading nation so far as co-operation with other nations in international fisheries conventions is concerned. This country has been a member of seven important commissions for a number of years. They include the Pacific Halibut Commission, the International Pacific Salmon Fishing Commission, the International Whaling Commission, ICNAF, the Great Lakes Commission and the North Pacific Fur Seals Commission. Most of these commissions have done extremely good work. I was pleased to note that the minister mentioned that action is being taken at the present time to bring about an international agreement with regard to the tuna fishery and regarding orderly fishing in the north Atlantic, having in mind safety and that sort of thing.
Speaking of safety, I strongly recommend to the minister that if he has not already done so he should set up an informal committee with the Department of Transport or take other appropriate action to make sure that fishing on the east coast especially, particularly during the wintertime, has adequate navigational aids and that the vessels concerned have adequate navigational equipment. In this way we could, so far as possible, prevent such tragic loss of life as that which occurred
Supply-Fisheries
this winter on more than one occasion as a result of the complete loss of small trawlers operating on the east coast.
The minister also mentioned briefly the importance of safeguarding, developing and expanding some of our most valuable species such as salmon on the east and west coasts. One of the best investments the Canadian taxpayer can make in terms of helping the economy is the expansion of means of increasing the stocks of salmon on both coasts, including the establishment of artificial spawning beds, the removal of obstructions and the prevention of pollution in salmon producing streams. This is a resource that has a very crucial link in its life cycle in the streams but does most of its growing in the high seas and comes back to our shores as a very valuable asset.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The minister did not mention other types of development of our fishery resources such as fish farming. If my memory serves me right, when the federal-provincial fisheries conference was held some years ago one of the important matters considered was that in some of the provinces at least there should be strenuous efforts to develop fish farming under certain circumstances, in the belief that it would be a viable and perhaps profitable industry in some areas. There may be a reason why there has not been much development in this phase of the industry. It may be that it is not as profitable or economic as was supposed at that time. Again, there may have been developments of which I am unaware. I do not want to take up any more of the time of the committee at the moment, Mr. Chairman, but I may have some further remarks to make when the specific items are called.

Even though he and I had a few differences of opinion occasionally, nevertheless I think he deserves that mark of commendation for the approach he took to the committee. This is the way a committee chairman should operate-fairly, justly and impartially while attempting to get the estimates passed and back in the house as quickly as is convenient. If the minister is posted to another place and having in mind his colleague the Minister of Labour that he is not going to run for election again, perhaps the abilities of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra should be kept in mind for the post of minister of fisheries if it becomes vacant in the foreseeable future. This would at least provide us with a minister of fisheries who is oriented to British Columbia, which has not been the case since 1957 when Jimmy Sinclair was the minister.
Perhaps a change of balance might do the department good. It would certainly have as its head someone who knows what the problems on the west coast are. I am not saying that the minister does not know them; I am just saying that he comes from the east coast. We desire these balances because cabinet members, as we know, are not particularly chosen on the basis of ability but on the basis of provincial distribution within the party which happens to be in office, plus a few other factors.
The minister raised a couple of points upon which I should like to comment, and I will toss into the hopper a few other items that are of great concern in the fishing industry. I wish to direct the bulk of my remarks to a peculiar and pertinent current situation in the fishing industry of British Columbia about which I have spoken to the minister on a number of occasions. The minister mentioned the necessity of international agreements and international concern about conservation and exploitation within the limits set by conservation. Many of us have put forward the contention for some time that there is a feeling amongst certain fishermen at home that we engage in the conservation of fisheries and restrictions upon our own fishermen in order that nationals of other countries may reap the 
benefits of our conservation measures. In other words, we hold back on fishing while somebody else reaps the profit. Whether this is valid is immaterial at the moment. The fact is that it is a matter of very great concern to certain of our fishermen at home and it is something to which we must give recognition. If benefits are to accrue from restraints upon our fishing industry for the purpose of conservation, we should be in the forefront of those receiving the benefits, especially where the conservation is carried out in our own territorial seas and fishing zones and in respect of those species such as salmon which breed in our streams.
We pointed out some years ago, even before the Soviet union became such a notable fisher off our west coast, the increase in Soviet union incursions into the fisheries on the Pacific coast and elsewhere. These came about partly because of the visit of the former minister of fisheries, Mr. Sinclair, to the Soviet union. Some of the information he was able to glean on his visit there was given a great deal of publicity and one could almost see the handwriting on the wall at that time. That is more then ten years ago now.
Regardless of the conflict that has taken place in mainland China in the last few months, we can foresee the time when China, as it develops and expands, will become a major nation involved in the fisheries of the Pacific Ocean. Whether we like it or not we will have to contend with that situation if and when it arises. I am confident it will arise because of the great need of people for food. As has been pointed out on a number of occasions, the ocean is perhaps the last known source of foodstuffs with special protein content that has not yet been explored and exploited to the full. When the minister speaks about the necessity of international agreements and international control or conservation these facts must be kept in mind so that we are prepared for these situations when they arise rather than try to cope with them after they have reached such proportions that we become greatly concerned about them.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Part of the problem, of course, has to do with the straight base lines to which the minister referred. The 12-mile fishing limit and the so-called straight base lines will not be as valuable to us as was thought by many people, even people in the fishing industry, some 10 or 15 years ago when pressures were exerted to establish a 12-mile limit. However, I submit for the minister's consideration, and
June 5, 1967

we have continued to point this out, that just before the bill was introduced in the Senate to establish the territorial sea or fishing zones a presentation was made to the government by the fisheries association. In that presentation the fisheries association delineated what they conceived to be the correct position of the straight base lines.
In so far as British Columbia is concerned, all people with any concern about or interest in the fishing industry whom I have met are of the unanimous opinion that the proposition put forward by the fisheries association should be accepted, namely, that the straight base lines should be drawn in such a way as to extend from the area along the northern tip of Vancouver island and around Cape Scott, the last point of land on the island, to the Cape St. James area at the lower end of the Queen Charlotte Islands, and from Langara at the northern part of the island up to the international boundary between British Columbia and Alaska. Thus the waters of Dixon Entrance, Hecate strait and Queen Charlotte Sound would be enclosed behind the straight base line.
The only nation with which we have been having discussions has been the United States and it is the only nation which has recognized historic fishing rights and has remained within the area regardless of the straight base lines. Therefore the only conclusion to which we can come is that our so-called negotiations have been about the location of the straight base lines, and any variation from the proposals put forward lay the fisheries association, which were endorsed completely by everybody in the fishing industry in British Columbia, which would designate more of that water area as international waters detracts from the position of the government. At that time the government claimed that it based its entire proposition for the 12-mile limit on the presentation made by the fisheries association, and that was the reason that it took action and made that particular proposal. I hope that whenever the announcement is made there is no variation on the landward side. This would be against the unanimous opinion of the fishing industry in British Columbia because we recognize clearly the necessity of taking in as much of that water territory as is possible for our own fisheries especially in view of the advances we have made in the last few years in the so-called bottom fishery which has been excluded by and large from extensive fishing.
Before proceeding to another matter I should like to say to the minister that during
Supply-Fisheries
the committee hearings last year, at which time intensive discussions were taking place between Canada and the United States, heated comments were made from time to time about the extent to which Alaskan or United States fishermen were catching salmon bound for the spawning grounds in the Nass and Stikine rivers in northern British Columbia. In other words, we were concerned about the extent to which United States fishermen were catching Canadian fish. At that time the final decision of the department was to conduct spot fishery research with a number of seiners, half a dozen, I believe, to attempt to determine the degree to which Alaskan bound salmon traverse what we hope will be our Canadian waters and the degree to which we might be able to catch the home-coming Alaskan salmon. The purpose was so that we might be able to present this information to the United States and say to them: "If you persist in establishing a surf line, not by agreement but by subterfuge and deceit, then we have no other recourse but to engage in extensive fishery of your home-coming fish because that is our only effective lever against you to make you draw in your surf line." That report has been made. I have not called the department to see whether or not I could obtain a copy of it, but there is no doubt that I can. I wonder in passing whether the minister might not feel disposed to table a copy in the house so that it would become a public document.
At the same time I should like to ask for the tabling of a similar document, namely, the report on research into the salmon fishery in the Stikine river. The Stikine river has its mouth in Alaskan waters and the salmon spawning grounds are in Canadian territory. Fish coming to spawn in the upper reaches of the Stikine and its tributaries must travel almost the entire distance through Alaskan waters once they leave international waters, and Canadian fishermen have no possibility of catching the fish until they actually get into the waters above the boundary between British Columbia and Alaska in the lower reaches of the Stikine river. This is another document which we should like to have.
There are other items which I shall not mention at present but will perhaps raise later. I should now like to spend what time I can dealing with the situation in Prince Rupert to which I have made reference and which I have discussed with the minister on a number of occasions. A couple of months ago reports reached us about the quarter of a

To do nothing is simply to play the "Nero fiddled while Rome burned" game, with Prince Rupert as the figurative pyre in this activity.
When the halibut season opened on May 9 there was further activity. Some companies refused to provide boats and ice to people who wanted to go fishing for halibut. Some companies were afraid that by so doing they would incur the enmity of one or other of the unions in the jurisdictional dispute and might be subject to having their plants picketed when the halibut boats returned. As a result fishermen were discouraged from going out to fish for halibut even though this fishery is an important part of the total fishery off the west coast. The mayor of Prince Rupert has persistently tried to find some way to resolve the dispute. Great credit is due him for persistently attempting to do this. I see you rising, sir. Perhaps my time has expired.

It is very kind of the committee and I shall try not to impose on its kindness. I shall shorten my comments. I became so involved in the matter that probably I went further than I should have.
I was about to say that the ministerial association had expressed its concern and has worked assiduously to find a solution. The housewives who have picketed in support of shore workers going to work to try to process fish as it was landed are to be given credit too. All those who participated in this action are to be commended, though so far not a great deal has been accomplished in the resolution of the dispute.
On Friday last-this is how serious this situation is-one of the unions, the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union, picketed the Prince Rupert fishermen's co-op plant because they said that the co-op was unfair or words like that. Before that the union had not declared particularly that certain plants were unfair, only that certain boats were unfair. Pickets also appeared at Royal Fish, saying that Royal Fish was unfair. These two companies were picketed by members of the United

Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union. The Deep Sea Fishermen's Union picketed on Friday at the Seal Cove plant of B.C. Packers, calling B.C. Packers unfair and saying that they would not unload the Fredelia III. The ship had to go to Royal Fish or somewhere else.
Here we have two unions, one of them picketing one fish plant and the other picketing another fish plant. The situation has resulted in members of one union involved in the picketing going through their own union's picket lines and in another case going through the picket lines set up by another union. This sort of thing in a community such as Prince Rupert, where trade union feelings run pretty high, could be damaging and explosive to say the least. This is a situation where friend turns against friend, union member against union member and neighbours do not speak to one another because they are on one side or the other of the dispute. The law has been ignored, and I submit that ignoring the law, as has happened in Prince Rupert, merely entices others to ignore it or to break it completely. When such a situation develops it simply cannot be tolerated. I do not care who thinks what about whose jurisdiction anything falls under. Threats of intimidation have been made against individuals by anonymous telephone calls. There is every likelihood that this situation will continue and that it may well develop into something worse.
In some instances people have been threatened with the prospect of being blackballed. This threat of the loss of opportunity to earn a living is one of the worst possible forms of intimidation. When I was with the trade union movement we condemned it as a scurvy practice when employers used it. I condemn it now and it should be condemned whether it is engaged in by employers or unions, and I emphasize the union's part in this. If any union or any person carries on a policy of such threats they should be condemned and, if necessary, restrained by law.
The only manner in which I can make this appeal is to the Minister of Fisheries. I submit that he must take action along the lines I suggested earlier or along some other lines but, for heaven's sake, the action must be taken soon. Otherwise the situation could explode and become something far beyond anyone's expectation. These situations have a tendency to do that when emotions run high and the economies and incomes of persons are involved.
June 5, 1967

I shall conclude by referring to the Inquiries Act. Section 2 of the act gives the minister and the government authority and jurisdiction to conduct some sort of inquiry into the whole problem. Obviously the provincial government has abdicated its responsibility by using semantics in the telegram it sent to the chamber of commerce. It ignored its responsibilities. Section 2 of the Inquiries Act reads as follows:
The governor in council may, whenever he deems it expedient, cause inquiry to be made into and concerning any matter connected with the good government of Canada-
I will not make humorous comments about whether we have good government.
-or the conduct of any part of the public business thereof.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The words "good government" are not capitalized. So I submit that the words "the good government of Canada" do not apply necessarily to this government or to any other government. The words refer in my opinion, to the simpler and broader concept of governing itself. Surely a situation which is imperilling a large number of people in one major seaport on the west coast should be of concern to the good government of Canada. When the force of law breaks down, as it is likely to break down, and when the force of law has been ignored, as it is being ignored, it is for the governor in council to cause an inquiry to be made into the good government of Canada and the conduct of any part of public affairs.
The time to act is now. Hon. members will find that there is no opportunity now to deal with this situation in depth and to study and examine it. A move in this direction would, I am sure, be supported by everyone in this house and by virtually everyone in Prince Rupert. The time has come to do something worth while. If we could set up a royal commission of inquiry in connection with that trollop Gerda Munsinger, surely we can have an inquiry into something as vital to our economy as the fishing industry in Prince Rupert.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to make a few observations on the estimates of the Department of Fisheries I certainly wish to thank the hon. member for Skeena for his kind remarks about me in regard to the chairing of the fisheries committee during the last session. It is a pleasure to hear such favourable comments about my behaviour in
Supply-Fisheries
the chair, especially after some of the comments made in the house with regard to my chairmanship of the defence committee, for which I got very little praise at times.
I am astonished that the hon. member should have gone so far, however, as to suggest I might even become minister of fisheries. I just want to say that we have at the present time an excellent Minister of Fisheries. Wherever I go I find him to be very highly regarded by working fishermen and people in the industry generally. When they talk about the federal government and of the Department of Fisheries they show a high regard for the present minister based on his understanding of the industry and the rapport he has with those who make their livelihood from it. I hope he will remain minister of that department for a long time.
It was interesting to hear what the hon. member for Skeena had to say about the deep impact made by the fishing industry on the social and economic life of the people who live on our coasts and engage in that industry. He expressed the situation well. It is a fact that this industry is virtually the life of hundreds upon hundreds of individuals in small villages and outports along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of Canada. Accordingly, when we review the estimates of this portfolio we are doing far more than considering a list of items setting out money which is to be spent. We are talking about the lives of a group of Canadians whose background is very different from that of most of us who come to this House of Commons. Few of us come from fishing villages and have felt the harshness of the lives that these people lead. So it is important for us to remember that we are dealing here with the livelihood of Canadians who earn their living in a dangerous pursuit, one which exacts great penalties in return for the yield it allows.
There are one or two items which have come to my attention as chairman of the committee upon which I hope the minister will comment briefly when he replies later to this debate. They have come from various sources. One concerns the complaints of fishing vessel owners in connection with subsidies for vessel construction on the west coast. I would refer to a letter I have received from Mr. Frank Buble, president of the salmon section of the Fishing Owners Association of British Columbia. It is dated January 22, 1967, and in one paragraph he states:
In 1966, 170 new boats came Into salmon industry mostly trailers and gilnetter's or combination boats (troll and gill net). This year it looks from reports

June 5, 1967
Supply-Fisheries
that there will be close to 300 more. When do we stop? The pie is going to be cut quite thin and this means more strikes etc. Is this good for our Canadian economy?
He goes on to say:
We find that most of our members have to compete with these new fish boats which enter the salmon, herring, halibut and trawling fisheries. We are not against subsidies but they should help all the vessel owners if they are to keep their boats and gear and electronic apparatus in first class condition without being a hardship on the owner.
This, of course, raises an old problem. When a subsidy for building something new is introduced some hardship is caused to those who are already in business and find themselves facing decisions about what to do with their own capital equipment. Many of these men have been in business for a long time and have made fairly large investments in boats which now have years of life behind them, though they are good for a few years more. These men are fighting for the equity they have acquired in their business. It is disheartening, I know, to find younger men entering a business assisted by special subsidies which were not available in the past. So when the question of subsidies is being considered, care must be taken to preserve equity as between the older fishermen who have already acquired their equipment and the younger men who wish to enter the industry.
It has been said that these subsidies were offered in the main to assist the boat-building industry. Yet there are still complaints on the Pacific coast that our vessel building industry is altogether inadequate compared with the industry in the state of Washington to the south, and that the subsidy has not assisted the efficient development of building techniques in Canada. I believe this whole subject needs to be reviewed in the light of some of the complaints which have been raised and some of the anomalies which have come to light.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I wish to refer now to a dispute which has arisen on the west coast and about which the last has not been heard. I have in mind the appeal made by sports fishermen for a net-free zone in the strait of Juan de Fuca. Many demands are being made by sports fishing clubs, chambers of commerce and the like, that a net-free zone be set aside from which commercial fishermen would be excluded, thus allowing them to engage in sports fishing. This idea is bitterly opposed by the commercial fishermen. We must face up to the fact that our population on the west coast

is growing rapidly, that more and more people are using small pleasure boats, sometimes for fishing and sometimes for cruising among islands, and these boats are creating a whole series of problems in relation to the fishing industry. They are creating wharfage and accommodation problems and are a disturbance when fishermen are working on the fishing grounds.
We cannot tell these people that they have no rights. Small craft and pleasure vessels are becoming a big business. They have to be regulated and it is our duty to study these problems more carefully in the light of changing conditions. I hope the minister will make some comment on the matter.
Recently I received a very interesting letter from the Fishing Vessel Owners' Association of British Columbia in regard to fish packed and sold in North America as "Greenland Halibut". The secretary of the association wrote me as follows:
We are writing to bring to your attention a matter that is of considerable concern to the halibut fishermen on the Pacific coast. As you know, halibut is a delicacy, commands a relatively high price and indeed it is not overstating the case to say that the name halibut itself is synonymous with a food fish of the highest quality. A very bad situation has developed in that a much inferior fish now taken in Atlantic waters and known, though not scientifically, as turbot, is being packaged and sold in North America as "Greenland Halibut". Compared to true halibut this fish is soft, mushy and oily but the housewife buying it in the supermarket or fish store and indeed the institutional buyer buying fish in large quantities is unable to differentiate, through lack of knowledge, between ''Greenland Halibut" at prices as low as 29 cents a pound and true halibut.
This is causing a good deal of consternation in the industry on the west coast and it is a problem which I refer to the minister with the request that he examine it. I understand there are international complications when we get into the question of marketing halibut abroad, but I hope the minister will give this matter his attention.
I have also received a letter from the Pacific Trollers' Association, one of the many organizations connected with the fishery on the west coast. It deals with the problem of pollution. It was sent to me by Mr. R. S. Stanton, secretary-treasurer of the association, and in it he wrote:
The Pacific Trollers Association protests the intention of the municipality of Richmond to discharge domestic sewage into the main arm of the Fraser River at any location, including the proposed Gilbert Road location.
Further, we protest against 16 permits issued by the B.C. Pollution Control Board to Richmond industries and businesses for existing outfalls, which
June 5, 1967



permit 3,688,300 gallons of domestic and industrial sewage to be discharged, daily, into the waters of the Fraser River.
This once more draws to our attention the increasing problem of pollution along our shores, both Atlantic and Pacific, as our population increases. Last year in the standing committee we drew attention to this question of pollution and directed the minister's attention to it in our final report. It is something which concerned all members on the committee. Could the minister assist us by letting us know what steps have been taken to combat the problem following receipt of the standing committee's report?
The hon. member for Queens, a man with long experience in the fishing industry and who was minister of fisheries at one time, referred to sealing. That question is dormant at the moment simply because the season is over, but we all know that the humane killing of seals will be engaging our attention next year. A few days ago I read the 1959 reports of the standing committee on agriculture dealing with the humane killing of food animals in slaughterhouses. They were interesting in relation to the seal problem. We cannot turn our backs on the fact that inhumane killing of seals is taking place. I believe that as a civilized people we have a duty to see that when animals are killed, something which is necessary to our economy, it is done in the most humane way possible. The reports of the 1959 committee on agriculture show the lengths to which the Department of Agriculture, veterinarians and other scientific people went in order to devise economic, effective, but humane killing procedures.
There is much to do in this area with respect to seals. I would urge the government to review the agricultural committee reports of 1959 and bring expertise to bear on the seal killing problem. The harvesting of seals is something which is related to the economic lives of fishermen, and we should come to grips with the problem that it has created. I am quite sure Canadians are capable of overcoming the difficulties and of satisfying people who were offended by brutal killing practices.
I cannot add much to what has been said so ably by the hon. member for Skeena in regard to the 12-mile limit, except to say that the industry awaits with expectation the efforts of the government to finalize the problem and to institute limits which will protect our growing coastal fisheries. The hon. member for Queens made reference to the possibility of establishing straight line co-ordinates
Supply-Fisheries
in some areas in order to start the work. I would concur in his suggestion because protection is needed for our fishing zones.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Anyone who has been to Expo and had an opportunity to visit the Russian building will have seen a vessel exhibited by the Russian fisheries. One of the most interesting exhibits is a Russian fishing vessel of about 40,000 tons. It has along its sides some 14 trawlers which can be lowered into the water. It is an enormous floating plant for deep sea fishing or trawling. To anyone interested in Canadian fisheries I would commend the Russian exhibit at Expo and I suggest that they think very carefully about the demand for protein in this world and consider the means that nations such as Russia have adopted in order to equip themselves with fishing plants so that they will be able to obtain protein. This means we are on the eve of a breakthrough in respect of obtaining food from the sea such as we have never envisaged. If we are to live with others in any kind of harmony we must learn how to practice conservation in concert with other countries and must make arrangements in respect of fishing zones and conservation in those zones on a scale we have not dreamed of before.
One of the first things which faces us in the years ahead is that we must learn how to share the food from the sea. There is a growing number of nations in the world which will have to turn to the sea in order to find the food for their populations.
In respect of our own committee on fisheries I believe it is generally agreed that members of the committee should be better equipped with expertise than they have been up until now. I should like to make an appeal to the government not only in respect of the committee on fisheries but in respect of all the important committees of the house that provision be made so that we will have much more expertise available to us in order that we can deal with these matters intelligently. We must be in a position to employ for a time on a regular or on a daily basis expert scientists, lawyers, doctors, veterinarians or whatever may be necessary in order to accomplish some of the work which faces us as members of committees,
I would hope that some time in the not too distant future, when we have come back after the summer recess, the minister would provide the committee on fisheries with a reference which would enable it to commence some of the studies I have mentioned and

June 5, 1967
Supply-Fisheries
some of the studies which have been suggested by the other members who have spoken in the house this afternoon. These are problems of great concern to Canadians and are of increasing concern the world over.
