Mr. Chairman, my intervention will be very brief. The hon. member for Skeena I believe spoke well with regard to the 12-mile fishing limit and the territorial waters. I recall that in the middle of 1964, I think, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in response to a question, said he hoped that before Christmas of that year the co-ordinates would be established. I was naturally pleased when finally the Minister of Fisheries announced today that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, within the next few days, will announce the co-ordinates and the base lines. I assume from that that all matters relating to the historic treaties and rights will have been studied by the time the announcement is made.
A very contentious question concerning the greater Victoria area has been referred to today by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. I am referring to the division of the catch of coho and Chinook salmon between the net fishermen, the trawlers and the sports fishermen. The problem arises basically because the International Salmon Fisheries Commission has no jurisdiction over these species. It remains more or less a problem for the Canadian government itself to solve. There has been a demand that a corridor be established around the coast of Juan de Fuca strait. Recently-I believe in an attempt to do something about the problem-area 19 and part of area 20 were closed to commercial salmon fishing. The fact is that this has made nobody happy. It has made everybody very unhappy. The fisheries council of British Columbia objected very strongly to this precedent of an infringement on the rights of the commercial fishermen. The trawlers objected that it did not help anybody except the net fishermen. The conservation council announced that its members were very unhappy because the closure stopped at the wrong point. As of today everybody is dissatisfied.
It seems to me that this is a difficult problem. Part of the problem, however, is that there is not sufficient knowledge concerning the habits of the coho and Chinook salmon particularly. More research is being carried out to establish the habits of these species, but basically I believe the problem is that not just the present minister but the department have not realized the growing importance of
[Mr. Deachman.3
the sports fishing industry. I realize there is a conflict and that a certain amount of the research must be carried on by the various interested groups.
In the attempt, which failed, to placate at least the conservation office I believe what was overlooked was the basic problem of the classes of fishermen on the Pacific coast and that there are too many fishermen for the resource which is allocated to them. If a solution can be found to this problem through licence limitation, I think the other problem of the division of the Chinook and coho between those interested can be solved also.
I suggest to the minister that the attempt to make and ad hoc arrangement will not succeed. Any such attempt will not succeed unless the other question of the limitation on licensing is also solved. I should like to repeat again that I think the importance of the growing sports fishing has been underestimated by the department, not only from the point of view of the jurisdiction of the department itself but also from the point of view of the over-all economy of the west coast and certainly in the area of Victoria.
My only other point concerns the wharfing facilities for commercial fishermen and more specifically the Victoria fishermen's wharf. I do not know whether the minister has received complaints in this regard. There has been, however, much publicity in Victoria. I have before me a petition signed by some 200 commercial fishermen. The preamble to the petition reads:
We the undersigned petition you as our federal representative-
This petition, incidentally, was also sent to the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.).
-to look into the inadequate wharf facilities for the Victoria commercial fishing fleet. The ever-increasing fleet demands more wharves, as at present boats are tied up four deep. This condition causes damage by passing traffic in the harbour and also creates a potential fire hazard.
I realize that the provision of funds for this purpose does not rest directly with the Minister of Fisheries. I submit, however, that the minister has a responsibility to carry out an investigation into this situation and then use his influence with the Minister of Transport in an effort to see that the necessary facilities are made available.
The following headline appeared in the Victoria Times of February 18: "Fishermen Hit Overcrowding at City Wharf." The news account itself is quite alarming. I have been down to see the situation and I hope the
June 5, 1967

minister will have a thorough investigation made, if he has not already done so, and use his influence with the Minister of Transport in order to provide adequate facilities.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
As to the fishermen's wharf at Shoal Harbour in Sidney, the fishermen have told me they would be prepared to pay additional wharfage fees if additional facilities such as lighting, individual berths, toilet and sanitary facilities could be provided. Again I suggest that the minister have his staff look into this and if they are satisfied that the fishermen would pay larger wharfage fees he could then use his influence with the Minister of Transport to provide these faciliites.
In closing I again urge the minister to put his mind to a consideration of the serious problems of conflict which exist between commercial and sports fishermen in the greater Victoria area.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to delay the passing of these estimates for any great length of time but there are one or two things upon which I should like to comment briefly while the estimates are before the committee. Let me mention in passing that I have had considerable dealings with the minister over the past 12 months and have always found him easy to get along with, co-operative and anxious to do what he thinks is best in the interests of the fishermen. There have been one or two exceptions, of course, regarding things I consider important and with which the minister did not agree, but I do not suppose we can always agree on all things.
The minister is in charge of a department of government which is very important to the people of many sections of Canada. Statistics indicate that the demand for our fishery products has never been greater than at the present time. There are, of course, several factors which contribute to this. One factor, and perhaps the most important, is the ever-increasing requirement of the world's population for food. Another is an evident increase in the appreciation and use of fish as a highly enjoyable source of protein. This I suggest is the result of insistence on quality in order to make fish competitive with other staple foods in places where there is a great variety of choice.
The third factor which is contributing to the greater demand for fish is the attractive manner in which fishery products can be and are being presented to the consuming public.
Supply-Fisheries
Fish is very appetizing and can be attractively presented. The minister and his department are to be commended for the work being done in the test kitchen of the Department of Fisheries. At the invitation of the minister I had occasion to visit that kitchen not long ago and I was very impressed by the work that was being done. They are making an effort to provide different types of recipes in order to prepare and present fish in a more attractive way. This is what we must do because fish is as appetizing as other foods but it has to be presented in an attractive manner. The department through its efforts at the test kitchen is doing a very fine job in this respect.
The consumption of fish is increasing. The latest figures I have from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics indicate that in 1963 Canadians consumed 137,000 tons of fish compared with only 113,000 tons in 1960. This augurs well for the future of our fishing industry. At the present time Canada is second only to Japan in the export of fishery products and stands either ninth or tenth in the world in total catch. Our annual total landings are over two billion pounds, worth over $160,000,000.
There are not as many people engaged in this industry as there should be, and one reason they are not taking part relates to the fact that some of the facilities for fishermen are unfortunately being neglected. This is particularly so in the area I have the honour to represent. This situation is not entirely the fault of the minister or his department but there should be closer co-operation between the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Public Works so that when repairs to wharves and other facilities at various centres are required they can be carried out quickly by the Department of Public Works. There must be closer liaison in this area.
Since I was elected to the house I have been hammering at the Department of Public Works to get some work done in the harbour and fishing centre of Georgetown. I have asked for a landing slip there so that fishermen can launch their boats without an undue amount of hard labour. This would not be a particularly expensive job, and I had hoped the Department of Public Works would accede to my request. I understand this request was also made by my predecessor who represented this same district. It is still my hope that somebody in authority will be able to persuade the Department of Public Works to

undertake this every important job required to assist the fishermen to carry out their work properly.
Other small construction jobs require to be done which will not involve great expenditures of money and are very important to those engaged in this industry. I hope that as a result of better liaison and closer co-operation these jobs will be carried out. I am sure the minister would be anxious to see these things done as long as they are for the benefit of fishermen.
Let me commend the minister for the initiative and courage he has shown in the setting of lobster trap limits for district 7B. I assure him that by far the majority of fishermen in the industry in that area are in favour of the trap limit. I carried out a poll, so far as I was able, to determine what their reaction was and I can say that almost unanimously the fishermen agree there should be trap limits. Since the fishing season opened I have spoken to them and they still agree this is a good thing, although there is some disagreement as to the number of traps. At the present time the number is limited to 500. I believe this is a test period and that probably the minister is awaiting reaction. No doubt he will receive that reaction before the season closes or the time comes to change the limit if it requires change. At that time I hope he complies with the wishes of the fishermen in this regard. On the whole the department and the minister are to be congratulated for encouraging trap limits, because this is what the industry and the fishermen require.
Let me say that I am getting sick and tired of all the complaints about the sealing industry. It is too bad that a very small minority of people can attempt to destroy an industry which is worth so much to so many people. The department has done everything possible to see that cruelties are not practised in the sealing industry and it is to be commended for what it has done. Extra protective staff have been employed and the minister has gone to the ice fields himself to see exactly what has taken place. He has also received almost daily reports while sealing was taking place. What more could he possibly do? The reports he has viewed confirm, in his opinion, that there is no undue cruelty. Why should men and women persist in making these allegations if there is no substance to them?

I was impressed by the report circulated by the minister's department a few days ago
[Mr. McQuaid.l
which gave a review of this industry. I hope it can be more widely circulated. I do not know how widely it was circulated but presumably it was sent to every member of the house. It should be more widely distributed because it points out very clearly and succinctly what the minister and his department have done so far as the protection of seals is concerned and alleviating cruelty in this area. The report also points out the value of the industry. I think it is high time we heard less of these allegations of cruelty which apparently cannot be substantiated to the degree to which they are alleged to be taking place.
There is one other point I should like to raise. It concerns the protection of the gear of inshore fishermen from the operation of drag-gers. We all realize that dragger fishing is a very important branch of the fishing industry and must be allowed plenty of scope within which to operate. I have always maintained that the inshore fisherman, the man who is trying to eke out a living in his small fishing boat and cannot venture too far from shore, must be afforded protection from the operation of these draggers. Unfortunately there is some destruction of inshore fishing gear by reason of the operation of draggers too close to shore. These offences are not being committed by every dragger fisherman. They are being committed by probably only a very small minority but that small minority is causing havoc to a great many inshore fishermen. The draggers drag over the gear of the inshore fishermen and destroy it.
I hope the department will engage a competent protective staff to protect the inshore fishermen in this regard and see that the draggers do not drag too close to shore. There is plenty of room further out at sea for them to operate. They are equipped in such a way that they can fish many miles from shore. The man in the small boat is not able to do this and has to stay close to shore in order to carry on his fishing. The grounds close to shore should be reserved for him and he should not have to run the risk of having his gear destroyed by dragging operations within the area in which he fishes.
Now I come to my main criticism. It concerns a point on which the minister and I apparently do not agree. I refer to the payment of the subsidy to those fishermen who build boats in the 35 foot to 45 foot class. I was not encouraged at all by the announcement of the minister today that 51 out of 96 applications from my province have been approved, four have been classified as doubtful and 41 have been rejected. I think I am

quoting the minister correctly. He said they did not meet the criteria established by the federal government or those established by the loan board of the province. This is exactly where the minister and I come to the parting of the ways.
I suggest that the minister cannot produce anything to convince me or the fishermen of my province that when the policy was announced in respect of paying a subsidy to those who build boats in the 35-foot to 45-foot class, any criteria at all were laid down. I do not think he can establish to my satisfaction that such criteria were laid down at that time. If there are regulations in this respect I invite the minister to place them on the record so we can examine them. Let us know the date on which they were passed and the date they were transmitted to the provinces and to the fishermen's loan boards of the provinces. I have made inquiries of the officials of the fishermen's loan board of my province, the boat builders and the fishermen themselves, and invariably they have told me that at the time the policy was announced in 1964 no such criteria or regulations were laid down other than that the boat would have to be in the 35-foot to 45-foot class and would have to be used for fishing other than for lobsters. These were the only two stipulations made at that time, as far as I can ascertain.
The minister has said there are other stipulations. I have not been able to find them. If there are any other regulations in this respect 1 should, as I say, be obliged if he would place them on the record so we may look at them and settle this question once and for all. Thousands and thousands of dollars have been lost to the fishermen of my province because they built boats fully expecting that the government would live up to its commitment and pay them the subsidy. They have built boats in the 35-foot to 45-foot class. At the very beginning the government started to pay this subsidy. Six fishermen were paid. I would like to know why they were paid the subsidy and others were turned down, because the boats they built were not one bit different from many of the boats which have been built since and in respect of which applications have been rejected.
Apparently the department picked these six names out of a hat. I do not know how they chose them. They were not picked on political grounds, they were not picked on religious grounds or because of the area in which they happened to live. The government will have to live up to its commitment in this respect, a commitment that was made and which the fishermen accepted in good faith. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is always a pleasure to say nice words about a maritimer, even if that is not always done by those from the maritimes. I started out today by complimenting the minister for the sizeable help his department has given the tourist industry in eastern Nova Scotia by the extension of the trout season in that area. I have written him a nice note to that effect, and now I say publicly what I have expressed privately. I hope he will be able to make a quick decision within the department about the possible extension of the salmon season, apart from the spawning grounds, well into the fall in that same area because fishing for sport can be built up on the eastern shore of Nova Scotia to the benefit of the population there.
Before I get to the main point of my brief address which will concern lobster trap losses I should like to ask the minister, as a humanitarian and a man of common sense, to exercise these faculties where they are not now bring exercised by the ministers of two other government departments. The first point concerns the Department of Transport. I see that the minister, a pseudo-maritimer smuggled in by Mr. Smallwood, has returned from his latest odyssey. I will be speaking to him when we deal with the estimates of his department concerning navigational aids which are of help to fishermen, but I hope the Minister of Fisheries will do something about the restoration of the Sambro lightship to its time-honoured position outside the approach to Halifax harbour. I am sure the minister has read in the fishing journals of the Atlantic provinces and in other publications how sorely the fishing industry feels about the loss of that particular navigational aid, especially in view of the Cape Bonnie disaster this past winter. I hope the minister will also use his influence with the Minister of Public Works to point out that by and large fishing vessels are growing larger and that a system of wharves which no doubt could cope with the problems of some 30 years ago is really not adequate if the fishing industry is to develop properly.

I could give many examples from my own constituency but I will content myself with two. The first one is Sambro, a wharf built in the days of the late prime minister R. B. Bennett. Sambro bids fair to become and could become the sword fishing capital of eastern Canada. Many fishermen from Sambro derive a handsome living from swordfishing, but many of these men have to travel in their boats an additional 20 miles to Halifax and land their catches at another wharf simply because the wharf at Sambro is not large enough. I suggest that the minister exercise his talents on the Minister of Public Works and have the Sambro wharf extension added to the estimates.
The other place is Little Harbour in the other part of Halifax county. It is one of those delightful, picturesque places of almost postcard tourist quality. It is a fine little harbour with a thriving fishing industry. However, it is being stifled somewhat because the government wharf facilities are simply not large enough for the thriving fishery there. I think the minister understands the point that when there are more and larger vessels it is time to bring the physical plants along the seashore up to date as well or the fishermen will suffer.
The main part of my brief remarks concerns the grievous losses suffered by lobster fishermen in at least that part of Nova Scotia which I serve and I understand also in other areas. Rev. Neil F. MacDonald of Musquodoboit Harbour has been good enough to compile for me a list of fishermen in specific areas, the number of traps they had set and the number of traps they have lost in the present season. I will send the list to the minister but I should like to say that the figures Mr. MacDonald has presented are truly staggering. For example, one fisherman at East Petpeswick had 115 traps set and lost every one of them.
Mr. MacDonald broke down his report into four different groups and on looking at them I found that at East Peteswick 729 lobster traps were lost out of 954 set. At an estimated value of $6 per trap this is a loss of $4,300 for the seven fishermen affected, or a loss of about 75 per cent of the traps they used for catching lobsters. This is a grievous loss. The effect on the community of one person's loss would undoubtedly not be as severe but the fact is that the whole lobster fishing population of a very small village has suffered this loss in the last couple of months. Mr. MacDonald's figures cover 53 fishermen who had
June 5, 1967	COMMONS
set 7,972 traps. Of these 4,236 were lost, or approximately 52 per cent. I worked it out for each fisherman. On the average there were 150 traps set of which 80 were lost. At an approximate cost of $5 or $6 per trap the loss was from $400 to $480 for each fisherman.
These figures may seem very insignificant but as the minister knows-he must have heard of similar circumstances in his own riding so I know this will appeal directly to him-a loss of that magnitude to men of these small means is a truly staggering one. It would be equivalent to the loss of half of one year's salary and expense allowance for a member of parliament. I suggest that we should take a new look at the assistance we can give to lobster fishermen, especially when their losses rise beyond what can be regarded as reasonable levels. Of course I am not in a position to state what I think is a reasonable level, but I would say that obviously a loss of 52 per cent is very unreasonable. We could establish a disaster fund, but it is too late for that. We could extend the lobster fishing season, but that is of no great help when the men do not have the traps immediately at hand to replace their losses. They have lost the equipment which gave them the opportunity to earn a living.
It is now six o'clock but I should like to conclude my speech with a very short observation. A few days ago the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg advanced the idea of a lobster trap depot. The movement of traps would be feasible because the lobster fishing season varies from one part of Nova Scotia to another. This was an idea which was developed in meetings with lobster fishermen in different parts of the Halifax riding by Mr. Buchanan, by my colleague from Halifax and by myself. I think it has some virtue. It would help the fishermen where the lobster trap insurance, generous as it is in certain aspects, does not. I hope the minister will consider my point and make some observations on it later in this debate.

speechtext:
That a special committee of the house be appointed to consider and make recommendations on a system of televising and radio broadcasting the proceedings of this house.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I hope the initial applause is an augur that hon. members will look with favour upon this resolution and permit it to come to a vote tonight.
I believe the question of televising the House of Commons proceedings is of particular importance to a country like Canada. Certainly it is true to say that the newspapers do an excellent job of covering the proceedings of the house. Though we may quarrel with their reports from time to time, especially when we feel we have been misquoted, by and large it is felt that a good part of the proceedings of this house are given coverage in the press. However, one thing that the newspapers cannot do for this house is to describe the special flavour of a nation whose people are bilingual, a flavour that is reflected
June 5. 196?
1158	COMMONS
Proposed Broadcasting of Proceedings in the debates here. I think it would be of enormous advantage to the people of Canada to realize the nature of the debates that take place, to hear these debates in one or the other of the official languages, and to witness the relationship that exists between our two founding peoples.
Again, Mr. Speaker, because we are a small nation in the presence of a large neighbour United States influence in this country tends to be very strong and is felt through the media of weekly magazines and television. We can use television to establish a better sense of identity in this country. It is the kind of medium of communication that would reach every corner of Canada and as such could counteract much of the American influence that is felt in this country.
Like all hon. members, I am very proud to participate in the work of this chamber. I never fail to be impressed by the fact that when I look around the house at the faces of the members and hear their accents I am looking at Canada. Words alone cannot convey this feeling to the Canadian people. I think it is important that they both hear these special accents and see those who speak them, a combination that makes up the mosaic that is our country.
A great speech is not only a news event; it is part of history. As history is written it should also be seen. We should have some way of preserving for those who come after us the words, the faces, the expressions and the emotions of the members of this house.
Think how important it would be to those attending school today to be able not only to read about the great figures of Canadian history but to hear their voices and see their faces as they deliver some of their memorable addresses. The events that have taken place in this house have implanted themselves upon history. We recall the pipe line debate, the debate on capital punishment, and the words of J. S. Woodsworth who alone spoke against the opinions which led this country into war. I am sure that each of us can think of hundreds of other occasions upon which figures in this house made their mark and whose voices should if at all possible be preserved.
Students visiting this house are quite often appalled by what they see here. They have the impression that every member of parliament sits firmly in his seat throughout the course of our proceedings, pays avid attention to every word that is spoken, that some kind of special debate and give and take occurs in this chamber to influence people on opposite
[Mr. Saltsman.l

sides of the house. Of course, this is not the way that parliament operates. One of two things would happen if the proceedings in this house were televised. Its image, which apparently is not liked by those who have seen it, would have to be explained to and understood and accepted by the public or this house would have to change its ways of operating.
I do not know which of these two things would occur but I believe that the decision about how this house should operate should take into consideration the opinions of the people that we were sent here to represent. None of us really knows who would benefit from the introduction of television in this chamber, but it is a new and important form of communication. Just as platform speakers are somewhat out of style in the new politics, perhaps some of the speakers who look good in print may not appear quite as impressive on television. This should not be any reason for limiting the kind of coverage that would take place in this house. Television would give a rounded perspective to what goes on and for that reason it would provide opportunities for all types of debaters and styles.
It is often said that members would play to the galleries. I think one of the things we have to face up to is that it does not require television in the house to make a member play to the galleries. This goes on all the time, and I think there is good reason for it. Much of what is done in this house is by way of informing public opinion and influencing public opinion. This can only be done by having the voices and opinions of the members of this house brought to the attention of the public at large. We know that what we say does not change opinions too much in the house. One of the great merits and virtues of publicity is that it will make our debates national debates and national dialogues. It is different in committees. There is more give and take, more willingness to accept opinions from whatever source they may come. Frequently there is a consensus. This behaviour the public should know about and see.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
Some have been helped by television, others destroyed. We recall all the comments which were made about the Kennedy-Nixon debate and how it favoured Kennedy. We should also remember the McCarthy army hearings and how the image, face and words of McCarthy practically destroyed him when the public had a chance to examine what he was saying and doing. Whatever the effect
June 5, 1967

may be on those in public life I think the public should be able to examine and to make their own judgments. We televise state visits, state funerals and the speech from the throne, all magnificent experiences for those watching.
I recall being present in the chamber and hearing one speech from the throne and seeing that speech later on television and being impressed by what I saw. I saw a great deal more on television that I had seen in the chamber that day. Television is a medium that can make the most minute scrutiny of events and should be permitted to do so. Canada led the way in 1957 in broadcasting the state visit of that year. It was rebroadcast in Britain later and received enormous public acclaim. That led to agitation in Britain for similar television coverage over there. That was a first for Canada. The practice was developed here and accepted in Britain. It is always nice to say that Canadians have done something first, and my suggestion to hon. members today is that we have an opportunity to create a first in the British parliamentary system by having the proceedings of this house televised.
In other countries there is radio coverage. The houses of Australia and New Zealand are covered by radio. The proceedings of the Saskatchewan government are broadcast. Municipal councils are covered by radio and those who have listened to such programs have been greatly impressed.
The big question is, how is this to be done? That is why I ask that the matter be referred to a committee so that the committee may examine the ways and means of televising the proceedings of the house. Another question that arises is whether such coverage should be continuous. Perhaps we should be thinking of the possibility of satellite television when it comes and of one channel being devoted all day to the House of Commons. One might ask: Who will listen to something like that? I think a great many would listen. I am impressed by the number of people who read Hansard from cover to cover. Similarly, many people in this country would be willing to follow the debates in parliament from start to finish.
We tend to underestimate the drama of this house and the fascination of its debates. No one will deny that there will be problems with editing. Those might be overcome by some system of party allocation, as with radio broadcasts. I cannot make any specific recommendations or suggestions tonight. I only ask that this matter be referred to a committee to
Proposed Broadcasting of Proceedings examine these questions and to make recommendations on them to the house.
What would the public see on some of these broadcasts? Let us admit that some of it would be pretty bad stuff. The words in the newspaper often make badly spoken words look good, but the words in the newspaper tend to be far more polite than the words on the original occasion. Viewers will see members reading papers, banging their desks, writing letters or perhaps asking a silly question. They might see or hear some of those private little "in" jokes that this house enjoys-private club jokes. They might see a house that is half full paying no attention to a member making a speech. It is those sorts of things that the viewers will see. Perhaps they will understand or perhaps they will not. But, much more important than that, the viewers will see the magnificence of parliament.
After they have overcome the initial shock they are bound to suffer from they will see what parliament is all about. They will see occasions they will never forget. I have been here for almost three years and there are occasions, debates and speeches that I shall never forget, and the same may be said of others who have been here. There is a great excitement in the chamber. As an example let me refer to the debate on capital punishment. There were speeches from all parts of the house, from members of all parties, that surely must have been among the most moving and thoughtful in Canadian history. I wish that all Canadians had heard those speeches as I heard them. It might have corrected some misconceptions.
We may remember the recent scandals that were headlined in every newspaper. The impression throughout the country was that this house was doing nothing but debating scandals, when the facts of the matter were otherwise. This house was occupied with other business and the scandal was being debated in the press and in a judicial process. All this the nation would have known had the proceedings of this house been covered by television.
Unpopular measures have been raised in the house. A number of years ago two members from my party raised considerable ire because of their conduct on the divorce question. Now some recommendations are to be brought forward to take care of this longstanding and obscured social problem. That process could have been hastened had the people of the nation been party to what was going on and had they heard the arguments that were presented then.

I wish there had been television in the house today. It was a proud moment for this house with the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) speaking and presenting his point of view on the war in the Middle East. The members of the opposition party responded. There was intelligence, there was concern and there was timeliness. The nation should have had the opportunity of listening to what was said at this critical time. I saw the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) being interviewed in the library. There would have been no need for him to be interviewed outside the House of Commons. He explained very fully how he felt about what was happening. Those words should have been heard directly by the nation from the house itself.
Many have spoken in favour of broadcasting the proceedings of the house. I believe that the views of three of our political parties are on record. My own party is on record as being in favour of televising our debates. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), who has often spoken on this subject, has even indicated, to his credit, that he has changed his mind with regard to it. The Prime Minister has told us he is giving serious consideration to this request. When the committee on broadcasting met a few months ago it hoped to have its proceedings televised but apparently that was not possible under the rules. And, if I may say so, even Your Honour has indicated an interest in this question-I believe a favourable interest.
I would therefore urge hon. members to give this matter serious attention, to realize that this great new dimension is here, and to take steps to ensure that Canada is one of the first countries to benefit from this new medium so that this house, with its unique French-English flavour, may be seen in a way in which it cannot be reported.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
subsubtopic: PROPOSED SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER BROADCASTING OF PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is evident that the proposal that debates in this house be televised is becoming increasingly acceptable to hon. members. As was mentioned by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) told us during the debate on the speech from the throne that he would be quite willing to consider this suggestion and thought we might make a start by televising the sittings of our committees.
In other speeches made during that debate many opinions were expressed, the majority of them in favour of the proposal. The subject was again debated while the estimates of the


Department of the Secretary of State were under consideration last week. I believe it was the hon. member for Okanagan-Revel-stoke (Mr. Johnston) who is in his place today, who opposed the idea of direct broadcasting. I rose to ask him whether he felt there was any real difference between reporting the proceedings of this house in the press and having them televised directly. He replied that he was disappointed I was not more familiar with the media, and recommended that I read Marshall McLuhan's book "Understanding Media".
I have read, or tried to read, not only "Understanding Media" but other works by Mr. McLuhan. While there may be linear, tactile, hot and cold media, that is not what I was getting at in my question. If we decide that the proceedings of this house are to be made public rather than kept private as they were at one point in parliamentary history, how do we rationalize our conclusion that they can be made public by means of a public gallery or Hansard or the press or commentaries by radio and television people, but may not be broadcast directly through television and radio?
Some critics of this measure say that if our debates were televised members of parliament would be more concerned with acting and playing to the gallery than with legislating. I think the stimuli for acting or playing to the gallery are with us now. We have a public gallery, we have Hansard, we have reporters. I do not see that the introduction of television would of itself bring about the type of behaviour suggested on the part of members. Direct broadcasting would amount to a change in degree rather than a change in kind.
If members of parliament are more concerned with acting than with legislation I do not think a solution would be found by limiting the types of media which report our proceedings. No doubt there would be problems. It might not be possible to televise all the proceedings from 2.30 until 10.30, in which case there would have to be editing. The question would arise: Who is to decide what shall be shown? We are, of course, faced with this situation now. We have no control whatsoever over the men and women in the press gallery who write about what goes on in the house. We have no control over the editors who decide which stories shall go on page 1 under headlines and which shall be buried on page 45. In any case, nothing is accomplished by restricting the media.
June 5, 1967

Personally, with respect to the responsibility of reporting what goes on in this house I should like to see something organized in Canada along the lines of the press council in Britain where the men who report the news have banded themselves together into a professional group to receive complaints from the public and discipline themselves if there has been a breach of their own ethical code. This might result in the public getting more truthful and factual information about parliament.
I should like to mention a few things which have happened because the proceedings of this house are not televised. One is that many television and radio stations stage their own debates with their own panellists. These debates are very often the only ones the public sees and hears. The real debate, which goes on in this house, does not always filter down to the public. What the public sees is "Platform" and other programs of that nature. I object to programs of this type being the main forum of debate. I do so because those who take part in them are not chosen democratically as are the members of this house. They are chosen by the people who organize the programs. If our proceedings were open to the public through television I think a lot would be done to bring public debate in Canada back to the House of Commons.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
If we look at the history of parliament we see that the arguments given both for and against the televising of parliamentary proceedings were given in the past with respect to admitting the press to the press gallery, with respect to the reporting of proceedings in Hansard, and so on. Hon. members who have studied the history of parliament know that originally the proceedings of parliament were held in private, and it was a breach of privilege to publish them in any way. Of course there were reasons for this in the early days of parliament. Members of parliament were afraid of the reactions of the crown to some of the things they might say in the house because in those days the crown was powerful. Members of parliament were also afraid of the reactions of the mobs.
It was only in 1641 that certain reports began to appear with the printing of votes and resolutions. Division lists were published for the first time in 1689, but even in 1696 the Commons ruled that it was a breach of privilege to publish the minority list in a division. This later changed.
DEBATES	1161
Proposed Broadcasting of Proceedings
At the time of James I any stranger coming into the room or chamber where the Commons sat had to take an oath that he would not tell outside the house what he heard inside it. The two arguments that we see throughout history being used against opening the House of Commons to the public were, first, that the speeches and the proceedings of the house would be misrepresented and, second, that if the proceedings were open to the public the members of the house would become more accountable to those outside the house than to those within the house. 1 think today most hon. members would agree the second argument would not have too much weight because a lot of us realize we are accountable to those outside the house. But the first argument, misrepresentation, is still the main argument used today.
In the early days some members took notes within the chamber in Great Britain and these notes found their way on to bulletin boards, into coffee houses, and into small printed journals. For a long while there was no press gallery. Members of the press had to sneak into the public gallery, and because the taking of notes was not permitted in the public gallery they had to try to remember what went on and print their reports from memory.
At the very beginning these reports were printed with fictitious names to get around the ruling on privilege. These reports would appear in the journals of the day with fictitious names, but the public knew they were reports of debates. The public came to know the fictitious names and to identify them with certain people in parliament.
Finally, in 1771 the matter came to a head when a man named Wilkes printed the names of people involved in debates. Breach of privilege was claimed in the house and certain delegations went to parliament on Wilkes' behalf. Finally the mayor and council of London were sent to the tower for taking his side. I would like to refer to a book published by the Hansard Society, "Our Parliament", in which this incident is reported. It says:
The corporation of the city of London, headed by the mayor and an alderman, both members, and inspired by Wilkes, championed the printers' cause. As a result the house committed the mayor and alderman to the tower. There they were so overwhelmed with visits, compliments and presents, that their imprisonment became one long ovation. There was no doubt on which side the public sympathy lay. After six weeks' confinement the prorogation released the prisoners, and a year later the sheriffs were able to boast with justification that the House of Commons had "tacitly
June 5, 1967
1162	COMMONS DEBATES
Proposed Broadcasting of Proceedings acquiesced in the claim made by London citizens on behalf of the public at large that the constituents had a right to be informed of the proceedings of their servants in parliament."
After this incident, reporting was still a breach of privilege but reports were published with impunity. However, reporters still had to go into the public gallery and were not allowed to take notes. A separate press gallery was only allowed with the rebuilding of the house after the fire of 1834. Finally, in 1845, by order of the British House of Commons, reporters were allowed to go into the press gallery and report the proceedings of the house.
This same debate continues today, and the same arguments, with respect to television and radio. A couple of weeks ago when this matter was being debated on another occasion, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) suggested that we might start with radio. I think I would prefer radio to nothing at all, but when we have television, which is a much more complete medium, I cannot see any reason why we should not use television.
As the hon. member who proposed this motion said, proceedings in the New Zealand House of Commons have been reported directly by radio since 1936, and it has proved a very popular program there. In Australia debates have been reported since 1946, but according to the commentaries I have read it has not proved as popular in Australia as in New Zealand.
In the United Kingdom in 1962 a private member's resolution was put on the order paper to provide for televising proceedings, and it was sponsored by 28 members of that house. The subject was again discussed in the United Kingdom during debate on parliamentary reform in 1963. During that debate the Times of London, of July 30, 1963, carried a full report in which was quoted the remarks of minister without portfolio, Mr. Deedes, as follows:
"What troubles me about the house," Mr. Deedes, minister without portfolio, has said, "is not its proceedings, but its communications.... There is a very big gap, too big for an informed democracy, between what happens in the house and what people think happens. This has led to suggestions that House of Commons proceedings should be televised."
The motion before us, Mr. Speaker, asks that this matter be sent to committee for study. This is a worth-while suggestion but I think it will only delay a decision. I would rather suggest that we start off on an experimental basis, allowing under your jurisdiction, Mr. Speaker, the televising of certain

proceedings of parliament, maybe the question period one week, maybe a particularly interesting debate another week, maybe some of the committees that would be of interest to the public a third week, and this at first without any general authorization that would be final.
I suggest it should be done on a temporary basis at first, and afterwards the house would have an opportunity to assess the results of the experiment.
In conclusion I would like to congratulate the hon. member for presenting this motion to the house. It gives us an opportunity to discuss the pros and cons once more. It is my personal feeling that some day the proceedings of the house will be televised, and the quicker we do it the better it will be, not only for us but for the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Yet I would say that we should not interpret the word "holiness" in the way some of our latter-day leaders have been attempting to interpret it, in the sense that we close ourselves off from the people and the world. I do not wish to become involved in a discussion of theology, but I should like to remind members that the root meaning of the word "holiness" is "healthiness", and this implies something about the body being vital and whole. If we prevent in any way whatsoever the people participating in knowing what is happening in this place, then we are doing a disservice to the house. If there has been-and I sense that there has been-over the past few years in this country a growing disillusionment with and despair about parliament and politicians, part of that I believe is due to the fact that we have cut ourselves off from the public. I realize that a hundred members could jump up and say that this is not true, on the ground that they send hundreds of letters to their constituents, have many personal visits with their constituents have many telephone conversations, and intercede on their behalf on many occasions. But that is what you are doing, in a sense, as a member outside this house.
June 5, 1967
1164	COMMONS
Proposed Broadcasting of Proceedings
I am talking about the decision making which affects the lives of the Canadian citizens. It is in that sense that the people feel cut off. I think it stems from being unable to participate in and know and see how in fact we represent them in deciding the affairs of state which affect their lives. So, if we are thinking of this place in terms of its sacred quality, or in terms of its importance to the country throughout history, then let us not give it a narrow interpretation but rather a broad and realistic one.
The second argument I think against broadcasting in this House of Commons relates to costs. I see figures, particularly those given by people writing in the newspapers, concerning how much it would cost. Surely the small cost in comparison to what it would do in terms of public enlightenment would indicate that we are being penny wise and pound foolish. The small amount of money that would be necessary to have set aside for the establishment of permanent radio and television equipment I do not think is a cost which we should bother ourselves about. Surely not, too, when we will be spending this year $140 million for one year's operation alone of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Also, as has been mentioned this evening, there is the concern some have that there would be some acting, if you like-some role playing, some playing to the gallery. Mr. Speaker, I suppose all of us to a degree are actors; otherwise we would not have gained a seat in this place. We have had to be adequate enough performers in our own area to convince a majority of the electors that we are necessary to them. I believe, however, that when we think of people who are playing to microphones or television cameras, we should not think only in terms of the negative effect but also we should think of the positive effect. Surely members will be conscious of the radio and television facilities in this house. Surely, when they rise to ask a question, make an interjection or make a speech, they will be conscious that their face and voice are going out across the country. That will be a good thing. Then maybe we will be able to cut out many of the questions and comments which have not been well advised. It may tend to eliminate some of the time which, in truth, I think is wasted in this place.
Perhaps, if great portions of the proceedings are broadcast-and frankly I do not argue for that-the people will be conscious of the fact that we spend too much time


debating matters of procedure and in allowing ourselves to be caught up in and concerned with matters of procedure rather than in dealing with the essential issues. I do not think it would do any harm at all to allow the public to have a much more constructively critical eye on how we govern ourselves in this place.
In introducing the resolution, I believe the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Saltsman) suggested that a channel should be set aside for the continual televising of our activities here. I believe the experience of countries which have attempted this with radio is that this is not a necessary step and in terms of its reward in fact might be too costly. I do not think there are many newspapers which furnish verbatim accounts of everything which goes on in this house. Even the best newspapers we have in this country and in others at best give a precis of the highlights of a day's session.
This is the kind of thing I should like to see presented both on television and radio. This, too, I think is an area in which people become concerned about the editing. Questions were raised in the Britsh parliament, and have been raised here in discussions concerning this question, about who would do the editing, and who would get to appear on the national news at eleven o'clock to ask his or her questions. Surely we do not say to any of the representatives of newspapers in the gallery, "Be sure to submit your copy to us in advance so that we will know you have given us a fair representation". We would rather have the opportunity to complain about it the next day, when we could read the papers for ourselves. We do not believe in effect that we should exercise this kind of censorship, because it is not in the interest of our system or concept of freedom. I think it might be a good suggestion made by the hon. member earlier to follow the procedure of a press council, such as obtains in Great Britain, where there is some kind of self-discipline imposed; but I would abhor any attempt on the part of parliament, government or any group arbitrarily to edit the news. These people are newsmen and they know what is news. They know what in fact will be of major importance to the public; and I think if we believe in the freedom of the press, this kind of decision should be left ultimately in their hands.
c (6:50 p.m.)
Naturally we know all too well from experience that when this freedom is trespassed and when licence rather than freedom exists in the press there is recourse still left in this
June S, 1967

house and the courts to take action of that kind. Therefore I for one would not fear the editing that would exist in the C.B.C., the C.T.V. or any kind of news agency reporting the proceedings of this house.
Finally I should like to refer to one of the objections that some members have had in the past, namely the fear that once they have said something on television or radio they would have great difficulty in correcting it, changing it or retracting it because there would be an immediate, once and for all kind of contact with the viewer or listener. Surely that is what we are trying to achieve in the modernization of our democracy. Surely the trouble in implementing so many of our decisions in recent years has resulted from the lack of communication, the lack of contact and the lack of involvement with the people of this country. It is not just good enough to lay down a barrage of material at election time when the public tends to be highly sceptical. We must have an on-going dialogue with the people between elections, so they will exercise their franchise competently and participate competently in this system.

Mr. Speaker, I admire the way in which the three previous speakers assumed that there is complete unanimity in this chamber on the subject, to the point of using up almost the entire hour. It would take a better speaker than myself, I am sure, to counter all the things that have been said in support of this resolution this afternoon in the minute or two left to me, but I will do what I can.
It has been stated that the public has a right to know, and that so-called right has been elevated to an absolute, it would seem. That process of elevation has been in evidence in the debate this afternoon. The right of the public to know has impinged very much on the right of privacy of the individual. This right to know, if television is allowed into this chamber under the guise of increasing the knowledge of the public, will impinge on the equally important right of this house to deliberation; and by that I mean to be deliberate, to take time, to be dull and to talk endlessly if necessary, and do all of those things that are bad television. Once we start televising procedures in this chamber I am sure we will not long be allowed to continue doing things that are bad television, because the medium will not stand for that.
The thing that concerns me most about the arguments presented this afternoon is the feeling that by televising this chamber it will
Proposed Broadcasting of Proceedings do all things, that it will be a panacea, that it can take off weight or put on weight, just like the old snake oil which promised everything. We are told that it will give the drama and the glory of this chamber. We are told on the other hand that bad aspects would be exposed. I wish some of the people arguing would make up their minds about which they are going to show, the drama and glory or the bad things which should be exposed. I am sure that, like all panaceas, which are not cure-alls at all, there will be a host of side effects which will be far more deadly to this institution, and will not be offset by the supposedly good things that will come out of this proposed move.
We on the North American continent are suffering from an urge to rush into history, and this is spreading to other parts of the world. We know the agony of public figures in the United States who have been concerned that the record be immediate and rushed out to the public. This has not meant that the people know any more of the truth of what actually happened, but confusion, bitterness and ignorance have all grown at the same pace.
We have an excellent example in this country of a very small institution that was one of the best in the country and rated high among those in the world, but which was virtually destroyed by television. I am speaking of the Leslie Bell choir. This was one of the finest we had, and it grew as a result of public appearances and radio. Once we had television it was natural to insist that this be brought to all Canadians through television. Mr. Bell found that he was no longer just a choirmaster, because he was told that people would not watch this choir stand idly singing, and that they had to move around. As a result to his great regret he became a choreographer at the same time, ultimately gave up televising and, in a sense, lost enthusiasm for the choir he had built up through different media.
For people to say that the effect is the same when you move from one medium to another is complete and utter ignorance, and is a misrepresentation of what by now should be obvious to Canadians. We were told the other night that television spared the United States from having Mr. Nixon as president. If it did that, then it was only an accidental byproduct. Those television debates showed North America that the thing that mattered in that contest was the rate of growth of the whiskers of the candidates. This became the important matter, and what happened afterward was only an accident.

June 5, 1967
Supply-Fisheries
I can give you an example of what has already taken place through televising, and I refer to the televising of the throne speech. Let me say only this about that situation. I was talking to one of the persons involved in televising that speech. He said the red carpets and red draperies will have to go because they bleed into the picture and everybody looks pink. I suggested that maybe it was the cameras that should be changed. That was heresy on my part: It was the chamber that would have to be changed; and if television comes into this chamber, the chamber will have to be changed. This is inevitable, and if it happens this will not be the same chamber.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few brief observations to make on the presentation of the estimates of the Minister of Fisheries. First I should like to express my appreciation, and I am sure the appreciation of all my constituents, for the recent gesture of the minister in extending the lobster Ashing season in district No. 4. This will no doubt be of great help in alleviating the very bad season experienced by the lobster fishermen in that area. Because of storms and bad weather conditions, their harvest to date has been perhaps only 50 per cent of the normal. The extension will at least give them a chance to recoup some of their losses. I am sure we in

that part of Nova Scotia are all very grateful for the gesture made by the minister.
At this time I should like to refer to the statement made by the minister in connection with the sealing operation in the gulf of St. Lawrence. I found it a careful, thoughtful and convincing statement which pointed out the importance of this industry to the economy of the area. The statement also pointed out very clearly that the seal hunt was being conducted in a humane manner. Perhaps there could still be some improvement in this connection and a correcting of some of the faults there may still be in the methods used to kill seals, but any reasonable person who takes the trouble to read the statement will be convinced that the almost world wide hysteria that has been aroused by some well meaning people, no doubt, but who have not taken the pains to see what has been done to improve the seal hunt, is completely unfounded. I feel that the statement must be publicized and brought to the attention not only of the Canadian public but the world at large, so that this criticism which has been such a reflection upon Canada as a whole may be dissipated.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
However, I think I would be remiss if I did not give full credit to the minister for having started the job of correcting public opinion on this subject. The people in my constituency are not interested in the seal hunt in the gulf of St. Lawrence but they have a deep sympathy for the people of that area and they realize only too well that the hunting of seal, which is a harvest just the same as the harvest of the domestic animals, which we all hate, is a vital part of the economy of that area.
I should like to appeal to the minister, who is undoubtedly interested in expanding the fisheries, to co-operate with me in my constant battle to get some action from the Minister of Public Works in the expansion of existing facilities. I would point out to him that in my constituency there is a need for new facilities or for an expansion of existing facilities because the fishing fleets have grown larger, and in some cases the facilities have fallen into disrepair.
There is another minor point which I should like to mention in connection with this, and that is that the planning of work, so far as dredging is concerned, is not well handled. For example we are now approaching the herring fishing season and a number of the wharves need dredging. They need it now, when the season is starting, not after the
June S, 1967

season is over or in the middle of it. I should like to ask the Minister of Fisheries whether he would consult me on some of these lacks and deficiencies and exercise some influence on his colleague in the cabinet, the Minister of Public Works. I will not name the individual items now because I do not think it appropriate, but I shall be very glad to bring them up in detail later in the course of the consideration of the minister's estimates.
I recall hearing the hon. member for Queens in his speech this afternoon make some comment on the increase in this year's estimates of the department. I observe that the increase over last year has been some 11.5 per cent, but I also note that the total amount is about one quarter of the total value of the 1966 exports of fish from Canada, which was about $219 million. I am not so concerned about the amount so long as it is worth while. It is a very substantial overhead figure and consequently it is imperative that it be well spent or we will indeed not get fair value in return.
Earlier in the debate mention was made of the east coast salmon fisheries. I should like to hear from the minister on what has been done or what can be done in connection with protecting the salmon in the Davis straits area, where I understand it has now been discovered they gather for their return to the east coast rivers to spawn. The salmon fisheries in the east coast, while not of the same tonnage proportion as those on the west coast, are extremely important to the economy of the maritime provinces, and it would be nothing short of tragic were protective measures not taken soon enough and in adequate proportions to protect this important item in the economy of the maritimes.
I have heard a number of comments from people in the western part of Nova Scotia on the question of the berried lobster, that is female lobsters producing eggs when in the pounds. I should like to hear from the minister as to why it would not be more practical and in the better interests of conservation to establish a system whereby the pound owners would be reimbursed for lobsters which they bought in good faith and under legal conditions for pounding during the season. When these lobsters are found to be in that condition they could be purchased and returned to sea. I have not at all been satisfied so far with any of the arguments against such procedure. I understand that the fish buyers pay a certain licence, which I believe is $1,000; but surely that cannot be a controlling factor in this matter, because the propagation of the
Supply-Fisheries
species should be far more important then the odd thousand dollars received in licence fees from pound owners.
I must emphasize that the 12 mile fishing limit continues to be an extremely lively and important issue in Nova Scotia, particularly in my constituency which lies in the western part of the province. While I appreciate the pre-occupation of the Secretary of State for External Affairs with a most vital issue at the present time, I hope that this temporary interruption of his attention will not result in a forgetfulness concerning the 12 mile limit for another year, two or three.

Mr. Chairman, 1 would like simply to ask the minister a question. As he knows, several hon. members have referred this afternoon to the seal problem, and the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra put forward a suggestion that possibly in the fall some matters in connection with the subject could be referred to the fisheries committee. As the minister knows, there is a group in Canada which has been campaigning very vigorously for the abolition of the seal hunt. I do not know whether it is numerous, but many allegations and demands have been made and even what I would consider to be some unnecessary language was used by these people. My point is that to a private member there seems to be many contradictory statements and many facts which I feel should be clarified. Therefore I wonder whether the minister would consider referring the whole problem of seal hunting in the gulf of St. Lawrence to the fisheries committee, which would not only study the problem of seal hunting but also the economic conditions and everything else that might pertain to seal hunters. There have been allegations that we could very easily do away with the seal hunt and that the sealers would still be able to find other means of employment. There has been a dispute over how much the sealers get out of seal hunting, and who benefits from the seal hunt, whether Canadians or people in other countries.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I think it would be worth while bringing these people before a committee so they could give evidence to support their claims. They would be subjected to cross-examination and re-examination and experts from the Department of Fisheries could also appear and give evidence. I think that then the public in Canada could be properly informed on all sides of this issue. As it is, the group that has been organized is going round the country

Supply-Fisheries
making speeches and showing films, and there is no one at the meetings to contradict them. I think it is better that they be brought before a committee which could question them and ask them to substantiate the allegations they are making publicly. I think such a reference would be worth while.
I would be interested in hearing the minister answer later, perhaps at the end of the estimates, whether this might be a worthwhile procedure.

Mr. Chairman, when we consider the estimates of the Department of Fisheries, we notice that the Canadian government makes a contribution to international research, allows subsidies for the construction of freezing and storage facilities and fishing vessels, and also subsidizes practically all fields of fishing. The department must be congratulated for that assistance which proves that the minister is really aware of the significance of the fishing industry in our country, a large country with thousands of miles of coastline on the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, vast inland seas and very great rivers. It is gratifying to see the enviable position our country has attained in the world markets with the assistance of the department. On both coasts of this country, that is, in the two areas where the fishing industry is the most important, the majority of workers have felt the need to organize and to protect their interests.
So now they are union members to negotiate better working conditions with their employers or again members of co-operatives to process and market their products.
Nevertheless, a certain number of Canadian fishermen are currently in a disastrous position, and I wish to call the attention of the minister to the fate of the commercial fishermen along the St. Lawrence river, below Montreal. In the constituencies along both shores of the St. Lawrence river, between Quebec and Montreal, fishermen can be found who succeeded very well in earning their livelihood and that of their families. These fishermen are not relying solely on luck but on organization. They own commercial equipment, hundred foot long drag seines or large traps, made of wire or various materials and called different names according to the areas.
To tell the truth, a fisherman does not fish. One might say that he draws from our resources, that he collects and loads his boat with hundreds, even thousands of pounds, and when the fishing is good, his catch may reach

one or more tons. In the past month, I have met several of those fishermen who told me in confidence that they were desperate in the present situation. As a matter of fact, the situation is more than desperate, it is tragic.
Those people who managed to earn $5,000 and sometimes $7,000 a year saw their earnings go down last year to as low as $600. And as things are going this year, that is, in 1967, if nothing changes, one wonders if they will manage to earn $100. And earnings of $100 for people who used to make $5,000 and $7,000, are really not a gift in this centennial year.
From Orleans island, near Quebec city, to Montreal, dead fish has been found on the shores of the river for a year and a half. Pike, pickerel, bass, carp and even eel are dying by thousands. Such a thing has been unheard of in the area in the last fifty years at least. We know that everything concerning water pollution is considered jointly by the central government and the provinces. However, I have to denounce the Expo corporation which has been polluting the river since 1965 and 1966. This is still going on, during the centennial year, since DDT or rather Rothane, if you prefer, has been poured in the river at the beginning of this summer; that is 2,700 gallons, or 27,000 pounds of violent poison.
Experts, paid to say that this violent poison is harmless cannot but agree that it is.
To the experts who are paid to say it is not dangerous, I who was paid to sell that violent poison for ten years as a salesman of insecticides to farmers, repeat that it is a violent poison and that the present situation is due to that poison dumped into the river continuously for the last three years. I hope that the minister will tell us what influence was brought to bear so that this criminal act, repeated by the people responsible for Expo, is condoned by the central government in Ottawa.
I also hope that the minister will tell us what the Department of Fisheries intends to do to help all those fishermen without another source of income, for those workers who are not asking anyone for anything and pay taxes like all other Canadians.
Will the minister tell us also what the cost will be to the Department of Fisheries because the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources neglected to assume its responsibilities before the damage had been done?
Mr. Chairman, I will deal briefly with this subject, in view of the fact that it is a matter of life or death for some fifty citizens living along the shores of the St. Lawrence. I ask the minister to make his views known on this, and
June 5, 1967

I hope all other hon. members representing riparian ridings will also make their views known on this situation.

Though we must be careful to protect our resources I do not know how much notice the fishermen received of the new policy. I know that the new salmon restrictions were published extensively, but I wonder how many of the actual fishermen, those who are engaged in the activity covered by the regulations, knew of the policy? They must be made aware of it for the policy to be effective quickly.

Supply-Fisheries

I wish to follow up what was said on another occasion by my hon. friend from Victoria-Carleton in connection with a subject which was mentioned also by my hon. friend from Saint John-Albert a minute or two ago, namely pollution of the Saint John river.
This is an important matter. The minister has told me that it is already affecting the salmon fishing and I am sure he agrees with me that the closest possible co-operation is needed, now, between his own department, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, and the provincial authorities.
Unlike most of the subjects with which we deal in parliament the answer, in this case, is clear. We know where the pollution is coming from. Seventy per cent of it is coming from Fraser Brothers in Edmundston. Another large portion of it comes from the capital city of New Brunswick which I am ashamed to say has done nothing tangible by way of removing the raw sewage it now dumps into the Saint John river. There have been surveys, I know, but as the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton said the other day, the subject has been studied to death.
The reason a New Brunswicker is concerned about this is that we in our province have had a tragic example of what can happen if pollution is unchecked in the loss of the salmon fishery on the St. Croix river. Only now are active steps being taken to redress this situation and I understand it will take decades, even generations, to restore that fishery.
As the minister knows, the case of pollution which concerns many of us has to do with the pollution which will arise when the Mac-taquac power dam is finished, building up a 60-mile head of so-called dead water-with the Fraser Brothers pollution entering the river above this point. There is really not much point getting civic minded municipalities and other groups to clear up their pollution if major corporations do nothing about it. This is not an indictment of Frasers; I know there are provincial and federal schemes-tax write-off provisions, and so on. But at some stage there has to be a deadline. Possibly

June 5, 1967
Supply-Fisheries
Fraser Brothers has already announced concrete plans so that deadlines will not have to be invoked.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
As I say, we know what the problem is. It has been studied backwards and forwards, or upwards and downwards, whichever way you prefer it.
